structure.title: Sustainability Statement
structure.heading: Sustainability Statement
structure.start_phrase:
Sustainability, which includes Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) dimensions, has 
been a central part of Deutsche Bank’s strategy since 2019.
structure.summary:
- What it is: A 2024 Deutsche Bank Group Sustainability Statement, combined with the parent company’s statement and included in the Annual Report. Sustainability is positioned as a core pillar of the bank’s corporate strategy and the “Global Hausbank” vision.

- Reporting basis and scope:
  - Prepared under German Commercial Code (HGB) Sections 315c/289c–289e.
  - Uses European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) as the reporting framework since CSRD was not yet transposed into German law at 12/31/2024.
  - Complies with EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures (Delegated Regulation 2021/2178).
  - Consolidated scope aligned with Group financial statements; no additional subsidiaries requiring inclusion.
  - Management of Deutsche Bank AG sets sustainability strategy and governance for the Group.

- Materiality and structure:
  - Topics determined via ESRS 1 double materiality assessment, covering upstream, own operations, and downstream value chain.
  - Organization of content:
    - General Information: Governance, Double materiality assessment, Sustainability strategy, Stakeholder engagement and thought leadership, Sustainable finance, ESG due diligence, Supply chain management (upstream).
    - Environmental Information: EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures, Climate change.
    - Social Information: Own workforce, Client centricity.
    - Governance Information: Culture, integrity and conduct; Anti-financial crime; Anti-competitive behavior; Tax; Public policy and regulation; Data protection; Information security.
    - Additional Information: Independent auditor’s limited assurance report; List of ESRS disclosure requirements complied with; Table of datapoints stemming from other EU legislation.
  - Sustainable Finance is treated as an entity-specific topic under ESRS 2 (no topical ESRS standard); Supply chain management maps to ESRS 2, ESRS E1 and ESRS G1.

- Strategy and positioning:
  - Sustainability embedded in governance, operations, products, and services since 2019; bank aims to support and accelerate the transition to a more sustainable economy.

- Key performance highlights and targets:
  - Sustainable finance: €373bn cumulative volumes since 2020; €500bn target by 2025 (excl. DWS).
  - ESG ratings (selected): CDP Climate Change B; ISS ESG C+ (decile rank 1/10); MSCI ESG AA; S&P Global CSA 67; Sustainalytics ESG Risk 24.8.
  - Environmental: Net‑zero emissions by 2050, with targets for eight most carbon‑intensive sectors in the corporate loan portfolio.
  - Social: Emphasis on equal opportunities, inclusiveness, and client centricity; ~70% Culture Pulse Index Score in 2024.
  - Governance: Focus on asset/data protection, preventing financial crime, and fair competition; >99% completion of mandatory trainings (AFC, Code of Conduct, Speak-ups).

- Reporting practices and assurances:
  - Comparative information provided; any alignment or restatement noted in relevant sections.
  - Use of ESRS 2 options to omit classified/sensitive information disclosed where applicable.
  - Policies referenced are available on the bank’s internal Policy Portal.

structure.title: General information
structure.heading: General information
structure.start_phrase: The Sustainability Statement of Deutsche Bank Group for the year ended December 31, 2024, which is combined with the parent company`s Sustainability Statement, was prepared according to Section 315c (1) in conjunction with Sections 289c to 289e of the German Commercial Code (HGB).
structure.summary:
- Scope and framework: Deutsche Bank Group’s 2024 Sustainability Statement, combined with the parent company’s statement, is prepared under German HGB Sections 315c and 289c–289e. As CSRD was not yet transposed into German law by Dec 31, 2024, the bank applied ESRS as the reporting framework per HGB allowances.
- Coverage: Disclosures span governance, strategy, impact/risk/opportunity management, and metrics/targets for material sustainability matters, in line with ESRS requirements.
- EU Taxonomy compliance: The statement fulfills Article 8 of the EU Taxonomy Regulation and the related Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178.
- Consolidation and scope: Prepared on a consolidated basis consistent with the Group’s financial statements; no additional subsidiaries require inclusion. Unless stated otherwise, disclosures for Deutsche Bank Group also apply to Deutsche Bank AG; specific entities like DWS are highlighted as needed. Deutsche Bank AG is the parent and most material component.
- Governance responsibility: Management of Deutsche Bank AG sets sustainability strategy and governance for both the parent and the Group; the bank operates globally via foreign branches. Workforce distribution details are referenced in the Combined Management Report.
- Materiality: Material topics and related impacts, risks, and opportunities across the upstream, own operations, and downstream value chain are determined through an ESRS 1-compliant double materiality assessment; process details are provided in a dedicated chapter.
- Report structure: Topics are organized under Environmental, Social, and Governance Information. General, cross-cutting chapters include Governance, Double materiality assessment, Sustainability strategy, Stakeholder engagement and thought leadership, Sustainable Finance, ESG due diligence, and Supply chain management (upstream value chain).
- Special treatment of topics: Sustainable Finance is addressed as an entity-specific topic under ESRS 2 (no topical ESRS exists). Supply chain management aggregates material upstream topics and includes disclosures under ESRS 2, ESRS E1, and ESRS G1.
- Comparatives and presentation: Prior-period figures are provided; any re-alignments to current presentation are noted in relevant sections.
- Omission of sensitive information: Where permitted by ESRS 2 BP-15(d) and (e), classified/sensitive or negotiation-related information may be omitted, with such omissions disclosed in the relevant chapters.
- Policies: Referenced policies are available internally via Deutsche Bank’s Policy Portal.

structure.title: Basis for preparation of the Sustainability Statement
structure.heading: Basis for preparation of the Sustainability Statement
structure.start_phrase:
The Sustainability Statement of Deutsche Bank Group for the year ended December 31, 2024, which is combined with the 
parent company`s Sustainability Statement, was prepared according to Section 315c (1) in conjunction with Sections 289c 
to 289e of the German Commercial Code (HGB).
structure.summary:
- Basis for preparation: The 2024 Sustainability Statement for Deutsche Bank Group (combined with the parent company’s statement) is prepared under HGB Sections 315c(1) and 289c–289e. Because CSRD was not yet transposed into German law as of Dec 31, 2024, the bank applied ESRS via HGB 315c(3) and 289d, covering governance, strategy, impacts, risks and opportunities, metrics, and targets for material topics. It also complies with EU Taxonomy Article 8 and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178.
- Scope and consolidation: Prepared on a consolidated basis with the same scope as the Group’s financial statements; no additional subsidiaries require inclusion. Unless stated, Group disclosures also apply to Deutsche Bank AG; specific subsidiaries (e.g., DWS) are highlighted where relevant. Deutsche Bank AG is the parent and most material component; it operates globally.
- Responsibilities and strategy: Management of Deutsche Bank AG sets the sustainability strategy and governance for both the bank and the Group. Related details are referenced to the Sustainability Strategy and Governance sections.
- Double materiality and structure: Material topics and their impacts/risks/opportunities across upstream, own operations, and downstream value chain are determined via ESRS 1 double materiality. The Statement is structured into Environmental, Social, and Governance sections, with overarching “General Information” chapters on Governance, Double materiality assessment, Sustainability strategy, Stakeholder engagement and thought leadership, Sustainable Finance (treated as an ESRS 2 entity-specific topic), ESG due diligence, and Supply chain management (upstream), the latter covering ESRS 2, ESRS E1, and ESRS G1 disclosures.
- Reporting practices: Prior-period comparatives are provided, with alignment notes where applicable. Classified/sensitive information may be omitted per ESRS 2 BP-15(d),(e), with disclosures indicating such omissions. Relevant policies exist on the internal Policy Portal. The Statement is subject to limited assurance by the independent auditor.
- Specific circumstances and methodologies: Deviations from ESRS 1 time horizons are explained in relevant chapters. Measurement uncertainties and estimates (e.g., financed emissions) are disclosed within topic-specific sections. Changes, corrections, or restatements are footnoted. The Statement follows the ESRS content index and includes datapoints from other EU legislation.
- Topics without specific ESRS: For entity-specific topics lacking a topical ESRS, metrics/targets use GRI standards: Data Protection (GRI 404-2, G4 FS4, GRI 418-1), Information Security (GRI 404-2), and Tax (GRI 207-4).
- Incorporation by reference (ESRS 2 BP-2 §16): Business model and value chain are in “Deutsche Bank Group” (Combined Management Report). Roles of Supervisory and Management Boards are in “Corporate Governance.” Information security governance/strategy/metrics/targets are in the Risk Report.
- Phase-in options: Use of ESRS 2 SBM-3 Par. 48(e) (anticipated financial effects) and partial phase-in for ESRS E1-9 (qualitative in first three years). Financial effects of sustainability matters are included in IFRS financial statements where required. Climate risk estimates did not lead to ECL adjustments for 2024 (see Risk Report).
- Events after reporting period: No material events affecting the Sustainability Statement.
- Governance highlights: Corporate governance roles are detailed in the Corporate Governance Statement. Sustainability governance includes the Management Board’s ultimate responsibility and the Group Sustainability Committee (one of eight MB committees), a decision-making body for sustainability across the Group (excluding DWS), chaired by the CEO with the CSO as deputy, comprising MB members, business heads, and key infrastructure functions, meeting quarterly.

structure.title: Governance
structure.heading: Governance
structure.start_phrase:
For information on the role and information provided to and sustainability matters addressed by, of the Supervisory Board
and the Management Board of Deutsche Bank AG please refer to the Corporate Governance Statement in this report.
structure.summary:
- Scope and context
  - Governance section of Deutsche Bank’s 2024 Annual Report outlining sustainability governance, oversight, incentive alignment, internal controls over sustainability reporting, and the double materiality assessment in line with ESRS/CSRD.

- Corporate and sustainability governance structure (ESRS 1; ESRS 2 GOV-1, GOV-2)
  - Ultimate responsibility for sustainability lies with the Management Board; Supervisory Board provides oversight and advice.
  - Group Sustainability Committee (a Management Board Committee) is the central decision-making body for group-wide sustainability matters (excl. DWS), chaired by the CEO with the Chief Sustainability Officer (CSO) as deputy; meets quarterly; oversees strategy implementation and alignment with corporate strategy.
  - Other Management Board Committees integrating sustainability:
    - Group Risk Committee: climate risk framework and monthly climate transition risk updates.
    - Group Reputational Risk Committee: escalation for reputational risks incl. sustainability.
    - Culture, Integrity and Conduct Committee: oversees culture and conduct incl. sustainability.
    - Group Investment Committee: reviews strategic investments incl. sustainability aspects.
  - Supervisory Board committees focusing on sustainability:
    - Strategy and Sustainability Committee: advises on strategies for sustainable development and responsibilities to society and environment.
    - Compensation Control Committee: links Management Board variable pay to sustainability targets.
    - Audit Committee: monitors reporting, internal controls, and ESRS implementation progress.
    - Risk Committee: oversees overall risk appetite and bank’s Sustainability Strategy.

- Chief Sustainability Office (CSO) mandate and organization
  - Reports to the CEO; drives sustainability strategy, regional governance, transformation program, policies/commitments (incl. human rights), ESG due diligence, regulatory interpretation, and stakeholder/ESG ratings engagement.
  - 2024 setup:
    - Strategy & Regional Governance.
    - Execution, Data & Regulatory.
    - Group Sustainability (stakeholder/ESG ratings spun out as a fourth pillar in early 2025).
  - CSO-led governance fora:
    - Sustainability Strategy Steering Committee (one of the bank’s Key Deliverables programs): seven meetings in 2024; escalates to Group Sustainability Committee or Group Operating Committee; tracks documented targets across cross-divisional workstreams:
      - ESG Financing; Empowerment & Training; Sustainability Data & Technology; Risk, Controls & Governance; Net-zero (CB/IB); Net-zero (Private Bank); Nature; Materiality analysis & reporting (supports CSRD/ESRS delivery and KPI integration).
      - All key deliverable milestones achieved by year-end 2024.
    - Sustainability Council: knowledge exchange; met four times in 2024.
    - Transaction/client-level fora:
      - Group Net Zero Forum (and divisional fora from 2024): evaluates transactions in net-zero target sectors, client transition assessments.
      - Sustainable Finance Governance Forum: interprets Sustainable Finance Framework and product classifications; may refer matters to Group Sustainability Committee or Group Reputational Risk Committee.

- Divisional and infrastructure enablement
  - Each business division has a senior sustainability lead and divisional fora.
  - Infrastructure functions with dedicated sustainability roles:
    - HR (culture, DEI, wellbeing), Procurement (supply chain/human rights), Global Real Estate (Scope 1–2 emissions and reporting), Technology/Data/Innovation (sustainability data/IT and tech decarbonization), Finance (Sustainability Reporting Team and internal control system for sustainability reporting), Risk (NFRM, ERM, reputational risk for sustainability), Compliance (policy updates for ESG rules, centralized ESG regulation sign-offs with Legal, training, marketing controls, greenwashing risk management).
  - Internal Audit provides independent assurance on risk management processes incl. climate and environmental risks.

- DWS sustainability governance
  - DWS Executive Board bears overall responsibility for sustainability risks/opportunities.
  - DWS Group Sustainability Committee implements the sustainability strategy across the platform and reports to the Executive Board.

- Regional setup
  - ESG Heads in Americas and APAC; Sustainability Coordinators across key markets (Europe, Africa/Middle East, South America, APAC) to align global initiatives; coordination with CSO’s Strategy & Regional Governance team via regional fora and senior governance meetings.

- Incentive alignment with sustainability (ESRS E1 related to ESRS 2 GOV-3)
  - Management Board compensation blends fixed pay with variable STI and LTI; balanced financial and non-financial targets; ratios set by Supervisory Board.
  - 2024–2026 LTI: 20% ESG component comprising:
    - Environmental: performance vs. published sectoral decarbonization pathways and risk appetite.
    - Social: increased female representation at MB-1 and MB-2 per German FüPoG II.
    - Governance: Control Risk Management Grade and AML/KYC remediation progress.
  - Supervisory Board (via Compensation Control Committee) designs and awards compensation; revised system effective Jan 1, 2024 and approved May 16, 2024.

- Internal controls over sustainability reporting (ESRS 2 GOV-5)
  - Management Board responsible; CFO oversees internal control framework; Audit Committee monitors process effectiveness.
  - Key risks: material misstatement and untimely publication; controls prioritize completeness and accuracy.
  - Multi-layered preventive, detective, and corrective controls; risk ranking based on impact and probability; four-eyes reviews, clear segregation of duties, comprehensive documentation, reconciliations, and analytical controls.
  - Evidence sources include regulatory audit reports, external auditor reports, and third-party reports; issues remediated promptly with oversight bodies informed.
  - As of Dec 31, 2024, no issues affecting completeness or accuracy of the Sustainability Statement were identified.

- Double materiality assessment (DMA) (ESRS 2 IRO-1, IRO-2, SBM-1, SBM-3)
  - 2024 DMA conducted in line with ESRS, covering impact and financial materiality on a consolidated basis with boundaries across own operations and direct suppliers/clients in the value chain.
  - ESRS disclosure requirements mapped to material topics; incorporates and reconciles DWS’s DMA.
  - CSO responsible for implementation; process follows ESRS 1 steps.

structure.title: Double materiality assessment
structure.heading: Double materiality assessment
structure.start_phrase: In 2024, Deutsche Bank conducted a double materiality assessment (DMA, the assessment) in compliance with the reporting requirements of the European Sustainability Reporting Standard (ESRS).
structure.summary:
- Scope and standards: Deutsche Bank conducted a 2024 double materiality assessment (DMA) aligned with ESRS (ESRS 2 IRO-1, IRO-2, SBM-3, SBM-1). It covered the consolidated Group (no additional subsidiaries), own operations, and the value chain limited to direct suppliers and clients. DWS’s separate DMA for Asset Management was considered and reconciled.
- Governance and ownership: The Chief Sustainability Office led the DMA. Clear roles, four-eye controls, content/plausibility checks, and a multi-level sign-off were applied: Senior Confirmation Officers, Group Sustainability Committee, Management Board, and Audit Committee.
- Topic identification: A comprehensive longlist was built from ESRS topics, prior material topics, sector frameworks/standards, regulations, voluntary principles, ESG ratings, NGO publications, and peer benchmarks. After consolidation, a shortlist of 14 topics with 33 sub-topics was created.
- IRO scoping and statements: Each topic was defined in Deutsche Bank’s context and mapped across the value chain at sub-topic level. Where topics did not trigger material impacts, risks, or opportunities (IRO) at specific value chain levels, rationales were documented. IRO statements were developed using desk research and subject-matter expert input.
- Evaluation methodology: Materiality was assessed for both impact and financial dimensions using severity and likelihood, considering scale, scope, and (for negative impacts) irremediability; financial evaluation included financial, reputational, and regulatory effects. A six-step qualitative scale, aligned with the Non-Financial Risk Management Grid, was used. Sustainability-related risks were not prioritized over other risk types; standard risk processes applied.
- Stakeholder engagement: Internal SMEs across businesses and functions evaluated topics; cross-cutting nature/human rights topics were addressed via workshops (Nature working group and Human Rights Forum). External stakeholders (clients, investors, a sector NGO, business associations) were consulted. Senior validation managers held structured interviews, especially on topics in the materiality threshold corridor.
- Thresholds and validation: Qualitative results were translated into scores. The materiality threshold was set at 3 on a five-point scale, with a 1.5–3 corridor for validation. Final material topics were determined by the Chief Sustainability Office, reflecting majority views from validations. A residual risk check found no highly likely severe non-financial residual risks tied to specific activities, relationships, products, or services.
- 2024 materiality results: A heatmap reflects impact and/or financial materiality by value chain, with color coding for above-threshold, corridor, and non-material dimensions. ESRS E2 (Pollution), E3 (Water and marine resources), and E4 (Biodiversity and ecosystems) did not meet the threshold in 2024, though the bank notes the growing importance of nature-related topics and is further developing its approach to Nature and Biodiversity.
- Changes vs prior years:
  - Digitization and innovation: No longer a combined headline; closely linked topics Information security and Data protection remain material individually.
  - Human rights: ESRS S2 (Workers in the value chain) and ESRS S3 (Affected communities) did not meet the threshold and are not disclosed in this Statement; broader human rights information is provided separately (Human Rights Statement; Human Trafficking and Modern Slavery Statement). Employee-related human rights remain material under “Own workforce.”
  - Client centricity: Introduced as an entity-specific, material topic; extends ESRS S4 (Consumers and end-users) beyond Private Bank to all client groups.
  - Anti-competitive behavior: Added as a material, entity-specific topic.
  - Non-material topics (e.g., Access and inclusion, Corporate social responsibility, In-house ecology) are no longer disclosed.
- Stakeholder views: User needs and affected stakeholder interests are reflected indirectly via SME evaluations and senior validation interviews; Investor Relations provided investor perspectives; business SMEs reflected client views.
- Sustainability strategy overview: Since 2019, sustainability is a core strategic pillar alongside macroeconomic shifts and technology. The bank embeds sustainability in governance, operations, products, and services across four pillars: Sustainable Finance; Policies & Commitments; People & Own Operations; Thought Leadership & Stakeholder Engagement. The strategy aims to contribute to the Paris Agreement and UN SDGs, with close linkage to nine SDGs and assessment of financing/issuance contributions to 15 SDGs via the Sustainable Finance Framework.
- Performance recognition: ESG ratings improved in 2024, including higher S&P Corporate Sustainability Assessment scores (notably in human capital), inclusion in DJSI Europe and Global, and MSCI improvements in employee KPIs and management of environmental impacts from financing.

structure.title: Sustainability strategy
structure.heading: Sustainability strategy
structure.start_phrase: Deutsche Bank sees it as its responsibility to support and, where possible, accelerate the historic transformation towards a more sustainable society and economy.
structure.summary:
- Deutsche Bank positions sustainability as a core strategic pillar since 2019, alongside macroeconomic shifts and technology, aiming to support the Paris Agreement and UN SDGs through four pillars: Sustainable Finance, Policies & Commitments, People & Own Operations, and Thought Leadership & Stakeholder Engagement.
- The bank links its strategy to nine closely aligned SDGs and assesses contributions to 15 SDGs via its Sustainable Finance Framework; ESG ratings improved in 2024, with inclusion in DJSI Europe and Global and stronger S&P CSA and MSCI outcomes.

Environmental
- Focus on facilitating sustainable financing and ESG investments; cumulative target of €500bn (2020–2025, ex DWS), with €373bn reached by end-2024, up 46% year-over-year; most volumes have an environmental focus.
- Frameworks underpin activity: Sustainable Finance Framework, Sustainable Instruments Framework, ESG Investments Framework; all updated in 2024; Transition Finance Framework to be implemented and published in 2025.
- Sector guidelines consolidated into a single policy; expanded sector targets include Aviation; Management Board long-term compensation partly linked to adherence to sector decarbonization pathways.
- Net-zero commitment by 2050 across Scope 1–3, with interim 2030 targets for eight high-emitting sectors and ongoing financed-emissions management.
- Client decarbonization approach: enable emission reduction, support business model transitions, and phase out not-to-abate activities (e.g., thermal coal).
- Nature-related work includes advisory panel guidance and #BackBlue ocean protection commitment; nature topics not yet material for detailed reporting.
- 2024 environmental highlights: €373bn cumulative sustainable finance/ESG investments (42% environmental), new Aviation target, comp linkage to sector pathways, strengthened ocean policies.

Social
- Integration of social outcomes into finance: at least €46bn classified as social and €91bn as environmental/social combined within the €373bn total (ex DWS); inaugural €500m social bond issued after expanding Green Instruments to Sustainable Instruments Framework.
- Social financing examples include social housing, hospitals in Sub-Saharan Africa, and support for just transition (e.g., Indonesia JETP); future emphasis on nature-based solutions benefiting communities and the environment.
- Human rights embedded across clients, suppliers, and employees, strengthening due diligence aligned with Germany’s Supply Chain Act and EU CSDDD.
- People strategy emphasizes learning (avg. €417 per FTE; 18.3 training hours per employee), internal mobility, leadership curricula (All-Managers-Curriculum, Leadership Kompass), health and wellbeing, hybrid work, and over 850 benefit plans.
- DEI focus with targets and programs for women and underrepresented groups; employee networks support diverse communities; leadership training on inclusive behaviors.
- 2024 People Survey: commitment 67% (down from 70%), enablement 70% (down from 71%); Boards identified focus areas: strategy & transformation, leadership, career development, performance & feedback; Culture Pulse Index at 69.89% (target 70%).
- Client centricity advanced via the “This is Deutsche Bank” framework and a bank-wide Client Centricity Program to improve collaboration, data/tools alignment, and resource allocation; robust product governance via New Product Approval and Systematic Product Review; NPS rollout completed in Germany.
- Social targets and 2024 outcomes: women to be at least 35% of MD/Director/VP by 2025 and 32.5% in top-two levels below Management Board by 2026; reached 33% women in MD/Director/VP by end-2024; Culture Pulse near target; strong client feedback initiatives.

Governance
- Comprehensive controls and frameworks for compliance, data protection, fair competition, anti-financial crime, whistleblowing, and risk remediation; annual assessments for antitrust, bribery/corruption risks; strengthened data privacy standards and policies.
- “This is Deutsche Bank” framework promotes a client-centric purpose, vision, strategy, and an aspirational culture anchored in four guiding principles and 16 behaviors; broad employee engagement via ambassador program and communications.
- Ongoing engagement with policymakers and industry bodies (e.g., Wolfsberg Group, German Anti Financial Crime Alliance) to improve conditions for clients and the sustainable transition.
- 2024 governance results: 99.8% completion of mandatory trainings; 100% of new managers completed speak-up training; 74 culture/integrity initiatives; enhanced perimeter security and security academy; revised data protection policy with further updates planned in 2025.
- Continuous monitoring of digital and AI-related risks and evolving regulatory requirements; regular antitrust risk assessments and control enhancements.

DWS sustainability strategy
- DWS focuses on climate-related investing, deepened engagement with investees and stakeholders, and advancing its own net-zero corporate transformation, while tailoring approaches to regional client preferences and regulation.

Stakeholder engagement and thought leadership
- Structured, ongoing dialogue with core stakeholders (clients, employees, investors, regulators, society) guided by a double materiality assessment; feedback channels include client complaints and whistleblowing.
- Client engagement through meetings, surveys, events, and publications; sustained demand for sustainable finance solutions across Corporate and Investment Bank and advisory transparency for private clients; partnerships (e.g., ORRAA, WWF).
- Employee engagement via People Survey, pulse surveys, townhalls, intranet, and networks, with targeted actions to address identified improvement areas.

structure.title: Stakeholder engagement and thought leadership
structure.heading: Stakeholder engagement and thought leadership
structure.start_phrase: Fair and open dialog with all its stakeholder groups is very important to Deutsche Bank.
structure.summary:
- Focus and scope: The excerpt outlines Deutsche Bank’s approach to stakeholder engagement and thought leadership and introduces its Sustainable Finance strategy and results, aligned with ESRS reporting and a double materiality lens.

- Stakeholder engagement framework:
  - Core stakeholders: clients, employees, investors, policymakers/regulators, media, and broader society (including NGOs).
  - Governance and process: responsibilities assigned across divisions/functions; feedback gathered via multiple channels (e.g., client complaints, employee whistleblowing) and integrated into strategy and business model.

- Clients:
  - Growing demand for sustainability advice, transparency, and products across Corporate Bank, Investment Bank, and Private Bank.
  - Engagement through meetings, surveys, events, digital channels, and publications.
  - Partnerships include Ocean Risk and Resilience Action Alliance and WWF.

- Employees:
  - Continuous dialogue via People Survey, pulse and exit surveys, townhalls, networks, and intranet.
  - 2024 survey showed declines in commitment and enablement; focus areas set: Strategy & Transformation, Leadership, Sustainable Career Development, and Performance & Feedback.

- Investors:
  - Expectations: consistent returns, responsible risk management, and transparent sustainability progress.
  - 2024 hot topics: execution of sustainability strategy; progress toward sustainable finance targets; climate/ environmental risk management; decarbonization pathways and net‑zero progress; sustainable finance opportunities; client transition in high‑emitting sectors; internal controls, compliance, and governance enhancements; DEI progress; ESRS implementation.
  - Ongoing disclosures via quarterly/annual reporting and a dedicated sustainability section on the IR site.

- Policymakers and regulators:
  - Active engagement through meetings, forums, and consultations; Government & Public Affairs monitors developments and shapes positions.
  - 2024 topics included Basel III implementation, EU macroprudential review, MiFID review, settlement cycles, securitizations, EU sustainable finance agenda, digitization, EU Banking Union/Capital Markets Union, Digital Euro, Retail Investment Strategy, UK listing/prospectus changes, UK Pensions Review, UK Wholesale Markets Review/MiFIR transparency, and US Basel III rulemaking.

- Media:
  - Emphasis on timely, open communication to support reputation and brand.
  - 2024 themes: sustainability strategy progress, climate risk management, environmental policies, sustainability reporting; #BackBlue ocean protection updates; responses to NGO studies; transparency on high‑carbon exposures; participation in interviews, panels, and media events.

- NGOs and broader society:
  - Dialogue on environmental and social issues; 2024 focus on climate change (incl. fossil fuel financing and energy transition), deforestation (notably in Latin America/Amazon and indigenous rights), and mining (including deep‑sea) with human rights, biodiversity, and climate impacts.
  - Case handling process: Group Sustainability reviews allegations, consults public sources and stakeholders, engages clients and civil society, seeks expert input, and may pursue remediation or exit; insights inform due diligence scope.

- Memberships and commitments:
  - UNEP FI (1992), UN Global Compact (2000), PRI via DWS (2008), Principles for Responsible Banking (2019), Net‑Zero Banking Alliance (2021).

- Sustainable finance strategy and performance:
  - Integral to the Compete‑to‑Win and Global Hausbank strategies; aims for global leadership.
  - Supports client decarbonization and climate adaptation; applies strict due diligence in carbon‑intensive sectors; aligns with EU Action Plan and the Paris Agreement; uses reporting and product innovation to drive impact and partnerships.

- Targets and 2024 results:
  - Post‑2022 achievement: exceeded the accelerated €200bn target (reached €215bn cumulative).
  - 2024 incremental sustainable financing and ESG investments: €93bn; cumulative: €373bn toward a €500bn target by end‑2025 (excluding DWS).
  - 2024 mix (incremental): Environmental €41bn; Social €9bn; Environmental & Social €28bn; Sustainability‑linked €15bn. By client type: Corporates €41bn; Sovereigns/Supranationals/Agencies €24bn; Private €18bn; Institutional €10bn.
  - DWS reported €163bn ESG AuM in 2024 (+€29bn YoY).

- 2024 sustainable finance milestones:
  - Updated Sustainable Finance Framework; launched Sustainable Instruments Framework (adding social asset categories to the Green Financing Framework).
  - Published 2023 Green Financing Instruments Report (allocation and impact on Green Asset Pool and liabilities).
  - Issued inaugural €500m social bond.
  - Published Deutsche Bank ESG Investments Framework.

structure.title: Sustainable finance
structure.heading: Sustainable finance
structure.start_phrase: The following chapter comprehensively discusses the subject of Sustainable finance.
structure.summary:
- Scope and strategic context: Comprehensive Sustainable Finance chapter aligned to ESRS cross‑cutting requirements (ESRS 2 and ESRS E1-4). Sustainable finance is a core pillar of Deutsche Bank’s “Compete to Win” strategy and key to the Global Hausbank approach.

- Targets and performance: After surpassing an accelerated €200bn target in 2022, the bank remains committed to €500bn in sustainable financing and ESG investments by year-end 2025. As of 2024 year-end, cumulative volumes reached €373bn excluding DWS, with €93bn incremental in 2024. DWS reported €163bn ESG AuM (+€29bn YoY). From 2024, market making (Q4) and pension plan assets (Q3) are included in group reporting.

- 2024 milestones and disclosures:
  - Updated Sustainable Finance Framework (SFF).
  - New Sustainable Instruments Framework (expanding green to social categories).
  - Green Financing Instruments Report 2023 with allocation and impact reporting.
  - Inaugural €500m social bond issuance.
  - Publication of the ESG Investments Framework (for Private Bank/AuM and pension plans).

- Governance and validation:
  - SFF sets global classification, eligibility criteria, due diligence, verification, and monitoring; updated in 2024 to reflect evolving regulations.
  - Deal validation uses a 6‑eyes principle; only SFF‑validated deals are reportable toward the €500bn target.
  - 2024 validation stats (Corporate & Investment Bank): 1,219 final decisions; 1,076 approved (Use of Proceeds 765; Company Profile 121; Sustainability‑linked 190); 140 declined; 3 referred/approved by the Group Sustainability Committee.
  - Sustainable Finance Governance Forum, chaired by the Head of Group Sustainability, guides SFF interpretation and application.
  - ESG Investments Framework harmonizes methodology for classifying Assets under Management and pension plan assets; DWS is out of scope due to its own policies.

- Training and awareness: Bank‑wide sustainability training rolled out, with division‑specific programs covering SFF application, transition/net‑zero, climate and nature risks, due diligence policies, and sales/advisory implementation. DWS maintains an ESG Education Framework and CE(S)GA platform (381 certified employees).

- Measurement methodology: Performance reporting follows industry practice across financing, bond issuance, market making, and investments (including pension assets). Volumes are apportioned by origination role; market making is based on annual average eligible bond inventory; investments on period‑end fair value. Activities are mapped to 15 UN SDGs.

structure.title: ESG due diligence
structure.heading: ESG due diligence
structure.start_phrase: Being a global bank supporting various sectors of the economy, Deutsche Bank can be potentially linked or exposed to negative environmental, social and governance impacts and risks.
structure.summary:
- Scope and approach: Deutsche Bank outlines its ESG due diligence across the value chain based on a double materiality assessment, with downstream processes governed by an Environmental and Social Due Diligence (ESDD) Framework, upstream processes covered under Supply Chain Management, and governance aspects in a separate Governance chapter. A mapping shows how the bank embeds the core due diligence elements (governance/strategy, stakeholder engagement, impact identification, action, and tracking/communication) across the Sustainability Statement.

- Environmental and social due diligence framework: 
  - Risk-based evaluation embedded in the Sustainability Strategy Implementation Policy and sectoral guidelines; refers matters with reputational implications to the Reputational Risk Framework.
  - Environmental criteria include biodiversity, water, waste and pollution, air quality, noise, emergency response; social criteria include human rights (child/forced labor, modern slavery), OHS, community safety, Indigenous Peoples and vulnerable groups, land/resource rights, and cultural heritage.
  - Governance risks (e.g., transparency, bribery/corruption) addressed via reputational risk and anti-financial crime frameworks.
  - Alignment with UN Global Compact, OECD Guidelines, UNGPs, IFC Performance Standards, and Equator Principles; participation in external initiatives (e.g., Cambridge’s BEI; WEF TFA on agriculture).
  - In-scope high-risk sectors/activities: metals & mining; oil & gas; thermal coal (mining and power); nuclear; hydropower; agricultural commodities & forestry; fisheries & marine aquaculture; maritime transport & infrastructure; Equator Principles transactions; other high-carbon, sensitive-area, deforestation, or human-rights–exposed activities.
  - Complementary provisions for tobacco (e-cigarettes, cannabis), defense, gaming, adult entertainment under the Reputational Risk Framework.

- Reputational Risk Framework:
  - Bank-wide process to prevent reputational harm via Unit RRAP, Regional Committees, and Group Committee escalations; oversight by Head of NFRM; DWS has a dedicated committee.
  - 2024 activity: 101 matters reviewed (vs. 106 in 2023); 72 handled only by Unit RRAP, 25 by Regional Committees, 4 by Group level. Matters with E&S issues: 7; gaming-related: 5; defense-related: 6.

- Minimum standards and positions (selected highlights):
  - Cross-sector: no engagement with substantiated material human-rights abuses without mitigation; no financing linked to deforestation of primary tropical forests; restrictions in/near UNESCO World Heritage Sites without governmental/UNESCO assurance.
  - Agriculture & forestry: no financing clearing primary tropical forests/illegal logging/illegal fire; no conversion of HCVs or peatlands; RSPO membership/certification (time-bound to 2025) and NDPE commitments.
  - Fisheries & aquaculture: no financing for recurring major quota breaches, unlawful or unlicensed activity; ASC certification for aquaculture by 2025 (time-bound plan).
  - Maritime: no financing of dredging harming sensitive habitats or destination projects in IUCN I/Ramsar/UNESCO Biosphere/critical biodiversity areas unless for protection; require compliance with UN/IMO/ILO E&S conventions.
  - Metals & mining: no direct financing of deep-sea mining; enhanced due diligence.
  - Oil & gas: no direct financing of new oil sands projects, Arctic projects (≥10°C July isotherm), or fracking in “extremely high” water-stress countries.
  - Thermal coal: no new or material expansion of coal power/mining/infrastructure; exclusions incl. mountaintop removal; in-scope criteria: ≥30% coal revenue, ≥10 Mtpa coal production, or ≥10 GW coal capacity; require credible transition plans (OECD by 2030; non-OECD by 2040); existing clients to present plans by 2025; new clients must have plans ex-ante.
  - Hydropower and nuclear: enhanced due diligence, potential exclusions; nuclear restrictions in certain jurisdictions.
  - Defense/controversial weapons, adult entertainment, gaming, tobacco: enhanced due diligence with defined exclusions (e.g., controversial weapons, certain firearms, prostitution, B2C online gambling where prohibited).

- Impact, risk and opportunity management:
  - Day-to-day transaction/client screening and strategic policy design overseen by Group Sustainability; training for frontline teams; footprint across Frankfurt, London, Singapore, Mumbai, New York, Washington.
  - Thermal coal guideline tightened in March 2023 (lower revenue threshold to 30%, introduce 10 Mt/10 GW absolute thresholds); 2024 portfolio review to assess client transition plans by 2025.
  - Nature workstream: 2024 ocean-protection updates tied to #BackBlue/ORRAA and UNEP FI Blue Economy Principles; new maritime transport/infrastructure guideline, stronger protections for sensitive marine areas, expanded fisheries to aquaculture, prohibition on direct financing of deep-sea mining. 2025 focus to include deforestation.

- Equator Principles:
  - Ongoing application to in-scope project-related finance; internal guidance/training; Group Sustainability support and external consultant use for higher-risk deals; escalation via Reputational Risk Framework as needed.
  - Participation in EP working groups (biodiversity, maritime assets, scope/governance).
  - 2024 deals at financial close: Project Finance categories A/B/C = 3/6/9; Project-Related Corporate Loans A/B/C = 1/3/7; selected disclosed projects include Woodfibre LNG (Canada), multiple Australian wind/solar portfolios, US BESS portfolios, Kao Data (UK), Senegal public lighting, and Salzgitter Green Steel (Germany).

- Training and awareness:
  - 2024: 102 relevant employees trained (2023: 104); Sustainable Finance Framework training available to front-office; awareness sessions for control and front-office teams on defense/gaming reputational risks.

- Metrics and reviews (no timebound targets):
  - Group Sustainability tracks transactional/client reviews to evidence effectiveness.
  - 2024: 925 reviews initiated (up ~27% vs. 2023), with a spike in agricultural commodities & forestry due to Trade Finance referral formalization and a new agriculture client; 817 decisions made, 794 approved, 15 declined, 8 referred to committees (all approved). Overall review ratio ~33% (2023: ~37.2%).
  - Equator Principles statistics provided for 2023 and 2024.

- Supply chain management (upstream focus):
  - Global Procurement leads supplier selection for spend ≥ €500k; Supply Chain Sustainability team embeds sustainability across the supplier lifecycle; oversight via management board, Chief Procurement Officer, and Chief Sustainability Officer.
  - Governance bodies include a Supply Chain Sustainability forum and a Third-Party ESG Oversight Forum (NFRM, Legal, Procurement, CSO).
  - Strategy integrates sustainability into end-to-end procurement; in 2024 the minimum acceptable ESG score for key suppliers was raised from 25 to 45/100 on EcoVadis (or equivalent from MSCI, Sustainalytics, ISS, S&P, CDP) to elevate standards, align with evolving best practices/regulation, and drive value chain impact; material topics from the bank’s assessment are embedded in the approach.

structure.title: Supply chain management
structure.heading: Supply chain management
structure.start_phrase: The following chapter comprehensively discusses the subject of Supply Chain Management.
structure.summary:
- Focus: Deutsche Bank’s 2024 Supply Chain Management, covering ESRS 2 (cross-cutting) and ESRS G1 (business conduct), plus related environmental and EU Taxonomy disclosures.
- Procurement model: Global Procurement leads supplier selection for annual spend ≥€500,000; Supply Chain Sustainability team embeds sustainability across the upstream value chain.
- Governance:
  - Management Board oversight; Chief Procurement Officer integrates supply chain sustainability in coordination with the Chief Sustainability Officer.
  - Supply Chain Sustainability governance body within Global Procurement.
  - Third-Party ESG Oversight Forum (Non-Financial Risk, Legal, Global Procurement, Chief Sustainability Office) for aligned decision-making.
- Strategy:
  - Sustainability integrated end-to-end in the supplier lifecycle.
  - Minimum ESG score for in-scope suppliers raised from 25 to 45/100 (EcoVadis or equivalent: MSCI, Sustainalytics, ISS, S&P, CDP) for ≥€500,000 spend.
  - Two material topics: Climate change and Business conduct (supplier relations, payment practices, information security).
- Policies and standards: Group-wide Procurement Policy; Supplier Code of Conduct (updated for evolving compliance and human rights expectations).
- Stakeholder engagement: Cross-functional collaboration, training/awareness on sustainability controls, and regular governance meetings with strategic suppliers.
- Climate change and decarbonization:
  - Active in CDP Supply Chain program; expanded CDP requests to 400 suppliers in 2024, covering 74% of supplier spend.
  - SBTi-aligned (not formally joined) target: reduce operational Scope 3 (excluding financed emissions, Category 15) by 46% by 2030 vs. 2019.
- Business conduct:
  - ESG clauses embedded in applicable contracts; suppliers must maintain a valid external sustainability assessment meeting the 45/100 threshold; collaborative corrective actions where needed.
- Risk assessment and screening:
  - Regular supplier risk assessments (including sustainability and information security); contingency plans for continuity.
  - Universal third-party screening (financial stability, sanctions/embargoes, internal watch lists, adverse media, PEPs), with escalation to risk control functions as required.
- Payment practices (Deutsche Bank):
  - Standard terms: 60 days (Europe), 90 days (RoW) for >€100,000; up to 30 days for smaller/EU general terms; local law observed.
  - 2024 metrics: average time to pay 32 days; on-time payments—<€100,000: 70%; >€100,000 Europe: 91%; RoW: 78%.
- Information security:
  - Third-party information security risks managed through a global TPRM program aligned with regulatory requirements (including EU DORA), supplier info-sec controls, periodic reassessments, incident notification, proactive outreach, and onsite assessments.
- Metrics and targets:
  - Supplier ESG KPI integrated into senior executive compensation; measures % of addressable spend with suppliers scoring ≥45/100.
  - Baseline 48%; focus on top 25 suppliers by addressable spend without ESG scores; centralized data repository; 2024 performance reached 61% (exceeding target by 3 pp).
- Asset Management (DWS) supply chain:
  - Own framework aligned with DB; responsibility in Third-Party Management.
  - Risk-focused procurement strategy; no formal public commitments.
  - TPRM includes environmental and human rights impacts; staged rollout; uses EcoVadis/proprietary data and annual adverse media screening; risk-based engagement and reassessments; SCDDA clauses applied proportionately.
  - Supplier Code of Conduct acknowledgment required for contracts ≥€100,000; RFPs require sustainability disclosures; approvals needed if past incidents.
  - Payment terms mirror DB; 2024 metrics: average time to pay 47 days; on-time payments—<€100,000: 62%; >€100,000 Europe: 75%; RoW: 76%.
- Environmental information snapshot:
  - Carbon footprint 2024 highlights: 98% of total emissions are Scope 3 Category 15 (financed emissions); high-emitting sectors include automotive (light duty), commercial aviation, steel, power generation, coal mining, oil & gas (upstream), shipping, cement.
  - Management Board long-term compensation linked to adherence to net-zero pathways in carbon-intensive sectors; overview of corporate loan exposure (drawn/undrawn) presented.
- EU Taxonomy (Article 8) disclosures:
  - Outlines six environmental objectives and DB’s best-efforts alignment of its Sustainable Finance Framework with the Taxonomy’s technical screening criteria.
  - ESG due diligence incorporates concepts akin to Do No Significant Harm and Minimum Social Safeguards.
  - Methodology for 2024: for use-of-proceeds, classify at transaction level; for general purpose lending to Taxonomy-reporting clients, weight exposures by clients’ Taxonomy eligibility/alignment turnover and capex KPIs (via MSCI data); identification of in-scope undertakings via a data collection project.
  - Notes evolving metrics and data limitations; aligned exposure reporting for climate mitigation/adaptation in 2024, remaining objectives from 2025.

structure.title: Environmental information
structure.heading: Environmental information
structure.start_phrase: The EU Taxonomy Regulation EU 2020/852 is aimed to allocate funding to environmentally sustainable sectors and support the transition toward a sustainable economy, setting out the guidelines and criteria for economic activities which financial and non -financial undertakings can classify as environmentally sustainable.
structure.summary:
- Context: Section of Deutsche Bank’s 2024 Annual Report outlining environmental information and Article 8 disclosures under the EU Taxonomy Regulation (EU 2020/852).
- EU Taxonomy overview: Explains the regulation’s aim to channel capital to environmentally sustainable activities and lists the six environmental objectives—climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, sustainable use and protection of water and marine resources, transition to a circular economy, pollution prevention and control, and protection and restoration of biodiversity and ecosystems.
- Framework alignment: States Deutsche Bank was an early adopter, aligning its Sustainable Finance Framework’s eligibility criteria on a best-effort basis with the EU Taxonomy’s technical screening criteria, particularly for climate mitigation and adaptation, with acknowledgment that criteria may evolve.
- ESG due diligence: Notes that the bank’s client reviews mirror the EU Taxonomy’s Do No Significant Harm and Minimum Social Safeguards concepts by assessing clients’ environmental and social management and performance.
- Business integration: Describes development of dedicated sustainable products, client engagement processes embedding Taxonomy considerations, and internal capability building through training on sustainable finance.
- Article 8 disclosure scope and timing: For year-end 2024, financial undertakings must disclose the proportion of EU Taxonomy-eligible exposures within covered assets, and report aligned exposures for climate mitigation and adaptation; disclosures for the remaining four objectives begin at year-end 2025.
- Covered assets definition: Total assets excluding exposures to central governments, central banks, supranational issuers, and the trading portfolio.
- Methodology for measuring eligibility/alignment:
  - Use-of-proceeds financing: Include exposures where the financed activity is Taxonomy-eligible/aligned.
  - General purpose lending: For counterparties subject to Taxonomy disclosures as of YE2023, weight exposures by clients’ Taxonomy turnover and capex KPIs.
  - Data sourcing and mapping: Collect turnover and capex KPIs via MSCI and map to counterparties.
  - Identification approach: Determine in-scope undertakings and their KPIs through a materiality-based data collection project; assets under management rely on external vendor classifications.
- Data caveats: Acknowledges evolving Taxonomy metrics and limitations in data availability and granularity.

structure.title: Disclosures pursuant to Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2020/852 (Taxonomy Regulation)
structure.heading: Disclosures pursuant to Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2020/852 (Taxonomy Regulation)
structure.start_phrase: The EU Taxonomy Regulation EU 2020/852 is aimed to allocate funding to environmentally sustainable sectors and support the transition toward a sustainable economy, setting out the guidelines and criteria for economic activities which financial and non -financial undertakings can classify as environmentally sustainable.
structure.summary:
- Scope and purpose: Extract from Deutsche Bank’s 2024 Annual Report (Environmental information) covering Article 8 EU Taxonomy disclosures and the bank’s climate change strategy and transition plan.
- EU Taxonomy overview: Explains the Taxonomy’s six environmental objectives (climate mitigation, climate adaptation, water/marine resources, circular economy, pollution prevention/control, biodiversity/ecosystems).
- Framework alignment: Deutsche Bank’s Sustainable Finance Framework is aligned, on a best-effort basis, to EU Taxonomy technical screening criteria (initially for mitigation and adaptation), with ongoing updates as standards evolve.
- DNSH and minimum safeguards: Bank conducts ESG due diligence similar to Taxonomy’s Do No Significant Harm and minimum social safeguards; notes EU Commission guidance (Nov 2024) that retail clients are not assessed for minimum social safeguards for immovable assets (e.g., residential real estate), and will monitor further guidance.
- Data and methodology:
  - Use-of-proceeds approach where known; for general purpose lending to Taxonomy-reporting counterparties, exposures are weighted by client Taxonomy turnover and capex KPIs sourced via MSCI.
  - Identification and KPI mapping prioritized by materiality; acknowledges data limitations as metrics evolve.
  - KPIs calculated on prudential consolidation scope and FINREP balance sheet.
- Households and real estate treatment:
  - Eligibility: residential mortgages, building renovation loans, and motor vehicle loans considered Taxonomy-eligible.
  - Alignment for residential real estate determined via EPCs and KfW programs: pre-2021 buildings aligned if EPC A or top 15% (concluded as KfW-70 or better); post-2020 buildings must be ≥10% below NZEB (concluded as KfW-40 or better). EPC collection is being expanded.
  - DNSH (activity 7.7): climate risk and vulnerability assessment based on external data and EBA Pillar 3 methodology; properties with very high physical risk deemed not aligned due to unverified adaptation measures.
  - Limitations: No current use-of-proceeds data for consumer loans; Taxonomy alignment for motor vehicle and renovation loan portfolios not yet available.
- Internal enablement: Ongoing development of sustainable products, client engagement processes, and staff training to embed Taxonomy considerations.
- Required Article 8 disclosures (2024 focus on eligibility for all six objectives; alignment for mitigation/adaptation only; remaining objectives from 2025).
- Key 2024 KPI results and movements:
  - Green Asset Ratio (GAR) stock: 1.0% (turnover KPI basis) and 1.2% (capex basis), down from 1.3%/1.5% in 2023 due to stricter residential real estate criteria.
  - GAR flow: 0.2% (turnover) and 0.4% (capex); methodology refined in 2024; prior year restated.
  - Financial guarantees: 2.4% (turnover) and 3.2% (capex).
  - Assets under Management: 1.4% (turnover) and 2.2% (capex).
  - Trading book and fees/commissions KPIs not required until year-end 2025.
  - Coverage metrics and exclusions disclosed per Annex V; noted rounding and template-based omissions.
- Climate change strategy and transition plan:
  - Net-zero by 2050 ambition; integrates risk management and business opportunity capture in the low-carbon transition.
  - Initial Transition Plan (Oct 2023) outlines definitions, methodologies, targets, and progress; aligned with ESRS E1-1.
  - Three decarbonization dimensions: own operations (Scope 1 & 2, including DWS), supply chain (Scope 3 Categories 1–14), and financed emissions (Scope 3 Category 15).
  - Portfolio decarbonization focus: sectoral 2030/2050 targets for eight high-emitting sectors; includes European residential real estate and corporate loan portfolios.
  - 2024 progress: Scope 1 & 2 emissions of corporates covered by targets reduced by 5 percentage points vs. 2023; Scope 3 emissions of the corporate loan book reduced by 4 percentage points vs. 2023.

structure.title: Climate change
structure.heading: Climate change
structure.start_phrase: For Deutsche Bank, reaching net -zero by 2050 means not only living up to its responsibilities, but also capitalizing on the business opportunities arising from the economy’s low -carbon transition.
structure.summary:
- Net-zero strategy and transition plan
  - Commitment to reach net-zero by 2050 with clear, quantifiable 2030 and 2050 targets.
  - Initial Transition Plan (Oct 2023) outlines methodologies, targets, governance, and progress; holistic coverage of own operations (Scopes 1–2), supply chain (Scope 3, Cat. 1–14), and financed emissions (Scope 3, Cat. 15).
  - Main levers: decarbonizing loan portfolios (focus on high-emitting sectors and European residential real estate), reducing operational energy use, sourcing 100% renewable electricity by 2025, cutting business travel and car fleet fuel, and using offsets for residuals.
  - 2024 operational Scopes 1–2 and Scope 3 Cat. 1–14 did not meet double materiality threshold for disclosure; details remain in the Transition Plan.

- Sectoral decarbonization targets and progress
  - Eight sectors with interim 2030 and final 2050 targets: Oil & Gas (Upstream), Power Generation, Automotive (Light Duty), Steel, Coal Mining, Cement, Shipping, Commercial Aviation (added Dec 2024).
  - Pathways used: IEA NZE 2050, Poseidon Principles/IMO Revised Strategy (Shipping), Pegasus/Mission Possible Partnership Prudent (Aviation).
  - Integration of targets into risk appetite; divisional carbon budgets and Net Zero Forums for transaction assessment.
  - 2024 progress highlights:
    - Oil & Gas Scope 3 financed emissions 19.2 MtCO2/y (−18% vs 2021 baseline; volatile).
    - Power Generation intensity 312 kgCO2e/MWh (−21% vs baseline).
    - Automotive tailpipe intensity 162 gCO2/vkm (−15% vs baseline).
    - Steel intensity 1,234 kgCO2e/t (−19% vs baseline).
    - Coal Mining Scope 3 4.6 MtCO2/y (−42% vs baseline; volatile).
    - Cement intensity 781 kgCO2e/t (+7% vs baseline; hard-to-abate, small portfolio).
    - Shipping: portfolio climate alignment marginally worsened YoY; 2024 to be reported next year.
    - Aviation: first portfolio alignment score 1.3% (2023 baseline).

- Financed emissions (Scope 3, Category 15) and methodology
  - PCAF-aligned calculations using client-reported and proxy emissions, mapped to loan commitments and EVIC; inclusion of Scope 3 client emissions changes sector rankings.
  - 2024 corporate loan book: Scope 1–2 and Scope 3 financed emissions detailed by top sectors; YoY changes driven by EVIC, data quality, FX, and portfolio effects.
  - European residential real estate financed emissions decreased from 2.5 to 2.2 MtCO2e/y; energy intensity improved; physical risk exposure low and mitigated by insurance; S&P hazard data used.

- Climate and environmental risk management framework
  - Embedding climate-transition, physical, and nature risks into BAU risk frameworks (credit, market, liquidity, non-financial), with enhanced risk appetite, divisional carbon budgets, early warning indicators, quarterly scenario reporting, and materiality assessments.
  - Credit processes include enhanced ESG due diligence for carbon-intensive sectors, transition and physical risk scorecards, watchlist triggers, collateral valuation standards, and insurance requirements.
  - Market risk monitors highly carbon-intensive traded exposures; weekly climate stress embedded in market risk appetite.
  - Liquidity stress incorporates climate disaster triggers; internal climate liquidity stress run.
  - Non-financial risk addresses greenwashing controls, training, and ESG integration.

- Scenario analysis, stress testing, and resilience
  - Use of IEA transition scenarios (STEPS, APS, NZE, Disorderly) and S&P/IPCC physical risk frameworks; in-house nature-risk scenarios across four nature themes.
  - Short-term financial impacts assessed as limited; medium- to long-term risks higher, with credit deterioration in fossil and high-intensity sectors, real estate valuation pressure, strategic/reputational impacts, and potential operational losses from physical events.
  - Static balance sheet assumption; economic capital add-on for tail carbon price shocks.

- Governance and oversight
  - Group Sustainability Committee (decision-making for sustainability), Group Risk Committee (oversees Climate & Environmental Risk Framework and appetite), Enterprise Risk Committee, Non-Financial Risk Committee, and Group Reputational Risk Committee.
  - Net Zero Forums (group and divisional) to assess high-impact lending vs targets; Management Board receives monthly financed emissions and alignment updates.
  - Compliance integrates ESG risk drivers and greenwashing controls; Internal Audit provides independent assurance.

- Policies, frameworks, training, and resources
  - Climate & Environmental Risk Management document underpins governance, appetite, monitoring, stress testing; complemented by Environmental & Social Policy Framework and Sustainable Finance Framework.
  - Extensive training on climate, nature, NFR ESG policy; resources allocated under sustainability change program workstreams (Net Zero Alignment Strategy, Risks/Controls/Governance, Nature).

- Nature-related (other environmental) risks
  - Early-stage methodologies; in-house identification of exposures across water depletion, terrestrial biodiversity/habitat loss, marine ecosystem degradation, and waste/pollution using SBTN and ENCORE tools with sector/country overlays.
  - Disclosed exposures by nature theme; total clients vulnerable to at least one type €30.6bn; continued engagement with TNFD and industry groups.

- Additional disclosures
  - Not excluded from EU Paris-aligned Benchmarks.
  - Rationale for not setting residential real estate net-zero targets; focus on client support, upstream sector targets, and policy engagement.

- Asset Management (DWS) client portfolios
  - Net-zero by 2050 ambition; climate-related disclosures via NZ Annual Disclosure and TCFD Climate Report; no standalone transition plan yet.
  - Thematic net-zero engagements focused on high-climate-impact sectors and Scope 3-intensive sectors; policies include ESG Integration, Proxy Voting, Coal Policy, and Real Estate Sustainability Framework.
  - NZAM interim target: 50% reduction in inflation-adjusted WACI by 2030 vs 2019; progress of 33.6% reduction (to 2022 emissions on 2023 holdings); notes on volatility and data lags.
  - Reported absolute Scope 3 portfolio emissions (ex. sovereigns and for sovereigns) and financed emissions methodology across asset classes.

- Social information (own workforce) opening
  - Introduction to HR governance and strategy: Global Head of HR accountability, leadership team, HR controls dashboard, and alignment of people strategy to corporate strategy with focus on fair, attractive working conditions, inclusion, and equal opportunity.

structure.title: Social information
structure.heading: Social information
structure.start_phrase:
Deutsche Bank’s own workforce is pivotal to achieving the bank’s corporate strategy, as its business model largely relies 
on its engaged and capable workforce, their ideas, skills, commitment, and well -being.
structure.summary: The excerpt from Deutsche Bank’s 2024 Annual Report (Social Information – Own workforce) outlines how the bank’s own workforce—defined under ESRS S1 to include employees and non-employees—is central to executing its strategy amid accelerating change from technology, globalization, sustainable growth, and evolving client needs. It details HR governance (ESRS 2 GOV-2): the Global Head of Human Resources is accountable for all HR matters, leads central, regional, and divisional HR teams, represents HR in bank committees, and ensures HR strategy aligns with corporate strategy and legal requirements, including anti-discrimination laws, reporting to the COO/Management Board. In 2024, the Global HR Leadership Team was realigned to strategic priorities, with heightened focus on Sustainability, Culture, Talent Sourcing, and HR Strategy. Risk oversight is conducted via a monthly HR Controls Dashboard tracking employment practices and control indicators across the employee lifecycle within the Non-Financial Risk Management Framework, with escalation and remediation governed by the Global Head of HR. The strategy section (ESRS 2 SBM-1/2/3, ESRS S1-1) explains that the people strategy derives from the corporate strategy and Global Hausbank ambition, is aligned with the bank’s purpose, and is shaped through engagement with internal and external stakeholders (e.g., regulators, trade/employer associations). Material impacts, risks, and opportunities focus on providing fair and attractive working conditions and an inclusive environment that ensures equitable treatment and opportunity for all; these assessments are reviewed annually with stakeholders. HR drives Human Capital Management to secure core competencies and to attract and retain talent, emphasizing highly committed, diverse employees with the right skills in the right roles at the right time to achieve strategic objectives.

structure.start_phrase:

structure.summary:
- Scope and importance
  - Focus on Deutsche Bank’s “Own workforce” under ESRS S1, covering employees and non-employees, as central to executing the Global Hausbank strategy.

  - Annual assessment of workforce-related IRO, linked to actions, metrics, and targets (including ESRS S1 metrics).

- Workforce engagement and voice
