  - Culture Pulse survey (3x/year) with 2024 Group KPI result 69.89% vs 70% target.
  - Additional channels: intranet interaction, townhalls, “Ask me anything,” and strong social dialogue with works councils (Germany) and European Works Council.
  - Whistleblowing framework (Raising Concerns Policy), non-retaliation, investigative protocols; Exit, New Joiner, and Speak-Up surveys support trust and effectiveness monitoring.

- Feedback culture and 2024 outcomes
  - People Survey declines in commitment (67%) and enablement (70%) amid transformation, with high intrinsic motivation; management focus on strategy/transformations, leadership, career development, and performance/feedback.

- Workforce management, size and structure
  - Headcount at Dec 31, 2024: 95,898; female 46.5%.
  - Largest locations: Germany (42.0%), India (23.5%), UK (8.1%), USA (8.1%).
  - Contract types (FTE): 99.7% permanent; part-time 7,911 FTE; Germany holds most part-time roles.
  - Non-employees (FTE) decreased to 6,369 (mainly IT vendor resources and contractors).

- Hiring, turnover, mobility
  - Top Employer certifications (Germany, India, Belgium). Inclusive Hiring Policy; dbCareers platform; strong graduate, internship, apprenticeship, and lateral/returner pipelines.
  - 2024 new hires 8,168 FTE; avg time to fill 77 days (55 for critical roles).
  - Total turnover 9.4% (voluntary 5.9%); higher in Americas and APAC; younger cohorts account for a larger share of turnover.
  - Internal mobility: 35.4% internal fill rate (69.6% for critical roles); €83m redeployment savings.

- Early career pipelines
  - 1,160 graduates hired; 376 vocational trainees (Germany/UK), with expanded dual study programs in digital/tech fields.

- Productivity and costs
  - Human Capital ROI: 60.7% (2023: 64.5%); total workforce costs €12.176bn; average revenue per FTE €334k.

- Working conditions, social dialogue, and change
  - Targeting Culture Pulse ≥70% as a proxy for working conditions.
  - Collective bargaining: in Germany (42% of workforce) 55.7% covered by CBAs; 100% covered by worker representation structures; restructuring managed transparently with social plans.

- Talent development and learning
  - Training spend €37.6m; 1.76m learning hours (48% mandatory); average 18.3 hours/employee.
  - Scaled AI and cloud upskilling (3,500+ AI fundamentals; 2,300+ cloud graduates in 2024).
  - Leadership Kompass; All-Managers Curriculum; First-time Manager and Senior Leadership Essentials; dbBOLD for Black talent; cross-divisional mentoring.
  - Acceleration programs: Directors (152, 42.8% women), VPs (374, 45.5% women).

- Performance and reward
  - Global Performance, Consequences and Reward Policy; sustainable, behavior-linked variable compensation.
  - Performance reviews mandatory; 2024 completion ~90% (female 88%, male 92%).
  - Annual total remuneration ratio: 237 (highest paid vs median).

- Work-life balance and benefits
  - Broad benefits (health, retirement, childcare, caregiving leave), available to full- and part-time where applicable.
  - 96% entitled to family-related leave; 20.7% of entitled employees took leave in 2024.
  - Hybrid work in 43 countries; up to two remote days where eligible; annual reviews of arrangements.

- Well-being
  - Four-dimensional well-being model; Global Well-being Hub.
  - Mental Health First Aiders increased to 737; manager e-learning launched; executive sponsorship and global events (e.g., World Mental Health Day).
  - External recognition (InsideOut Award; top employer rankings).

- Diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI)
  - Global strategy across: Accountable Leadership, Attracting Diverse Talent, Inclusive Culture, Equitable Development & Advancement; integrated in Code of Conduct and Hiring Policy; robust ERGs and external partnerships.
  - Gender: statutory board targets met (Supervisory Board 35%, Management Board 20%); goals of 30% women at MB-1 and MB-2 by end-2025; “35 by 25” senior title goal at 33.0% in 2024; STEM 29.9% women; revenue-generating management roles 27.1% women.
  - Gender pay gap (global, unadjusted) 38.8%; adjusted 6.0% (driven by seniority/location mix); ongoing equal pay measures and 35 by 25 initiatives; UK pay gap continued to narrow.
  - Age diversity: under 30 (16.2%), 30–50 (57.0%), over 50 (26.9%).
  - Disability inclusion: 3,057 employees globally (Germany 6.2% of headcount); accessibility and accommodations; SGEnable Enabling Mark Platinum (Singapore).
  - Racial/ethnic diversity: UK Black heritage representation reached 3.7% (up 23% vs 2021 baseline); dbBOLD development program expanded.
  - LGBTQI+ leadership recognition and awards; neurodiversity network and partnerships (e.g., Autistica UK).

- Incidents and complaints
  - Code of Conduct training 100% completion.
  - 57 upheld/partially upheld incidents of discrimination/harassment; 202 additional complaints on discrimination/harassment/working conditions; €0.25m total fines/penalties/compensation; consistent disciplinary process and linkage to reward.

- Transition to client centricity chapter
  - Client-centric purpose, vision, and strategy across Corporate Bank, Investment Bank, Private Bank, and Asset Management.
  - ESRS S4 “consumers and end-users” adapted to financial institution context; focus on information-related impacts (access to information, privacy, freedom of expression) and excellent client experience.
  - Governance foundations for product responsibility anchored in the Code of Conduct and policy framework.

structure.title: Client centricity
structure.heading: Client centricity
structure.start_phrase: Having served clients for more than 150 years, clients are at the core and center to Deutsche Bank’s business.
structure.summary:
- Central theme: Deutsche Bank’s client centricity framework, purpose, vision and strategy anchored in serving clients’ lasting success, with a sharpened, client-focused business model across four divisions (Corporate Bank, Investment Bank, Private Bank, Asset Management) and regional layers.
- ESRS alignment: Disclosures guided by ESRS 2 and ESRS S4; double materiality assessment finds ESRS S4 “information-related impacts for consumers/end-users” material. “Consumers/end-users” mapped broadly to all client types beyond private individuals; data privacy addressed separately in Governance Information.
- Governance for client centricity: Code of Conduct approved by the Chief Compliance and Anti-Financial Crime Officer; extensive group-wide policy framework; distinct governance for product responsibility, client satisfaction and complaint management.
- Client Centricity Program (strategy): Bank-wide collaboration around priority clients, alignment of client data and tooling, improved resource allocation to drive Shareholder Value Added; goals include increased client penetration and product density; enhanced tooling leveraging AI; 2024 progress includes cross-division priority client identification and target client system design (relationship vs. mass market), with ongoing rollout into 2025+.
- Impacts, risks, opportunities: Positive impacts from suitable, transparent products/services and fair practices; opportunities in satisfaction, loyalty and reputation; risks from inappropriate sales/communications and conflicts of interest.
- Product responsibility framework:
  - Suitability/appropriateness: Global policy setting minimum standards, controls, warnings, metrics to the Non-Financial Risk Committee; divisional product governance; new product approval and regular product reviews overseen by Non-Financial Risk Management.
  - Selling practices/marketing: Business Communications Policy mandates fair, clear, accurate communications (e.g., balancing benefits and risks) aligned to MiFID; divisional controls (e.g., pitchbook checks) and risk assessments.
  - Conflicts of interest: Group policy, divisional conflict registers, Business Selection and Conflicts Office oversight, Employee Compliance Program for personal transactions, Compliance Control Room for inside information; incentives linked to conduct.
  - Retail lending safeguards: Private Bank affordability assessments, early client notifications and hardship mitigation.
  - Training: Mandatory Code of Conduct, communications, conflicts, suitability/appropriateness; additional consumer-protection training for German retail staff; non-completion impacts compensation.
- Client satisfaction approach by division:
  - Corporate Bank: Client Service Teams (CSTs) coordinate coverage and monitor relationship performance; Corporate Cash Management surveys since 2018 (>1,500 client responses in 2024), scope expanded to Trade Finance & Lending and German Mid-Corp.
  - Investment Bank: Uses internal/external data, broker reviews and client meetings; dedicated Client Strategy teams in FIC and O&A; CST framework applied.
  - Private Bank:
    - NPS as core metric, reported regularly and localized by region/channel.
    - Germany: Deutsche Bank brand NPS 67 (FY 2023: 63) from ~165,000 responses; 76% promoters; Postbank brand NPS 13 post-Unity migration, with call center NPS improving by 21 points (from -19 to 2).
    - Italy/Spain/Belgium: Revenue-weighted NPS 13 (FY 2023: 8) from ~24,000 responses.
    - Wealth Management (global): ~2,100 responses; ~75% promoters; revenue-weighted NPS 67; unweighted overall NPS 71.
  - Asset Management (DWS): Global top-client NPS survey; 2024 score 53 (2023: 50); findings drive continuous improvements and training.
- Complaint management (global framework):
  - Group-wide Client Complaints Policy and Procedure (aligned with ESMA/EBA guidelines and BaFin interpretation), with unit-specific KODs; scope, logging, escalation, reporting, timelines, and roles defined; monitoring of closures, handling time, and redress, with ≥10% changes analyzed; ability to complain about the complaint process itself.
- Complaints by division:
  - Corporate Bank: KOD owned by Divisional Control Office; severity categorization, aging and quality reviews; monthly Complaints Oversight Forum; streamlined 2024 focus on higher-risk/escalated complaints; 2024 complaint volume down 8% YoY; top root causes: operational, communication, application issues.
  - Investment Bank: Policy, Procedure and KOD define ownership/logging/escalation; monthly reviews by business and Compliance; 2024 logged complaints up 56% YoY due to better coverage/training and surveillance checks; root causes include operational issues, trade execution and pricing/fees.
  - Private Bank: Localized complaint functions compliant with global and local rules; prompt logging, assignment, and privacy-compliant handling with 2nd line involvement as needed; overall complaints down 18% YoY.
    - Germany Personal Banking: New complaint inflow down 23% YoY as Postbank IT migration issues tapered; service levels normalized, focus on mortgage lending remediation.
    - Wealth Management Germany: Slight YoY increase; mostly execution/settlement and service; no systemic patterns.
    - Spain: New inflow up 120% due to Supreme Court ruling on mortgage fees; handling times normalized by Nov 2024 after staffing/tech remediation.
    - Italy: Complaints up 6% due to KYC remediation-related account restrictions.
    - Belgium: Complaints down 7% after Quality Council remediation.
    - India: Complaints down 37% after data-quality and frontline training improvements.
    - Data privacy: <1% of complaints related to third-party breaches were substantiated; none systemic.
  - Asset Management (DWS): Central Compliance-owned Group Complaints Policy with KODs, supervision via Global Supervision Framework and WSP; materiality criteria defined; 2024 complaints down 40% vs 2023, majority from retail fund investors; prior spikes linked to protest mail actions.
- Metrics and oversight: Complaints metrics reported to divisional management and Management Board; suitability/appropriateness metrics monthly to the global Non-Financial Risk Committee; business-level trend analysis and remediation planning.
- Culture, integrity and conduct (governance linkage):
  - Code of Conduct as behavioral foundation supporting client-centric purpose; emphasis on speak-up and ethical behavior.
  - Culture, Integrity and Conduct Committee (Management Board-mandated) oversees the framework across the Group.
  - Three Lines of Defense underpin risk culture and governance; continuous regulatory monitoring and policy/process adaptation.
  - Training and capability indicators: 100% of new managers completed speak-up training; >99% anti-bribery/anti-corruption completion; 74 culture/integrity initiatives; 2,492 AFC employees in a standalone second line of defense unit.

structure.title: Governance information
structure.heading: Governance information
structure.start_phrase: Culture is how Deutsche Bank’s Management Board members and employees behave daily and the key driver for achieving the bank’s purpose, vision and strategy.
structure.summary:
- Emphasizes culture as the daily behaviors of Management Board members and employees, central to Deutsche Bank’s purpose, vision and strategy, and foundational to trust, reputation, and long-term success.
- Highlights trust as essential yet fragile, stressing the risks of misconduct, unethical behavior, and silence (lack of speaking up).
- Describes governance via a dedicated Culture, Integrity and Conduct program overseen by the Management Board’s Culture, Integrity and Conduct Committee.
- Notes committee leadership and composition: co-chaired by the MB member for Corporate Bank and Investment Bank and the MB member/CEO Americas; includes representatives from all business divisions and key infrastructure functions appointed by responsible MB members; female representation is 3 of 13 voting members.
- Outlines strategy and framework (ESRS 2 SBM-3): the committee oversees a framework that defines, communicates, and reinforces cultural aspirations and behaviors, embedding sustainable performance aligned with laws, regulations, and internal policies and procedures.
- States the framework’s group-wide scope across all businesses, geographies, and infrastructure functions.
- Connects culture with risk governance: Deutsche Bank commits to continuous learning and improvement, with culture supporting effective risk management.
- Affirms use of the Three Lines of Defense model as integral to the bank’s risk culture, with roles and responsibilities detailed in the bank’s risk management framework (as referenced in the 2024 Annual Report – Management Report – Risk Report).

structure.title: Culture, integrity and conduct
structure.heading: Culture, integrity and conduct
structure.start_phrase:
Culture is how Deutsche Bank’s Management Board members and employees behave daily and the key driver for achieving
the bank’s purpose, vision and strategy.
structure.summary:
- Focus: Deutsche Bank’s governance of culture, integrity, conduct, and anti-financial crime as reported in the 2024 Annual Report.
- Governance structure:
  - Culture, Integrity and Conduct Committee (CICC) oversees a group-wide framework; co-chaired by Corporate/Investment Bank MB member and CEO Americas; representatives from all divisions/functions; 3 of 13 voting members are women.
  - Culture is embedded across the Group and linked to the bank’s purpose, vision and strategy; trust and speaking up are central.
  - Risk governance anchored in the Three Lines of Defense per the Risk Report.
- Strategy and framework:
  - CICC mandate: define, communicate, reinforce cultural aspirations and behaviors; ensure adherence to laws, regulations, and policies.
  - Culture seen as a driver of trust, performance, ROI, brand value, and competitive advantage in client/employee attraction and retention.
- Impact, risk and opportunity management:
  - Strong speak-up and raise-a-concern mechanisms viewed as creating positive short-term impacts; absence assessed as a likely short-term societal harm and medium-term business risk (loss of trust, higher costs, potential loss of license).
- Raise a Concern, Whistleblowing, Speak Up:
  - Raising Concerns (including Whistleblowing) Policy owned by Compliance; annual review; encourages reporting of violations and criminal activity.
  - Whistleblowing Central Function (within Anti-Financial Crime) handles concerns; confidential handling; quarterly trend reporting to senior management and Supervisory Board Audit Committee; ad hoc notifications for highest-risk cases.
  - Multiple channels: management, control functions, HR, Integrity Hotline (anonymous where permitted), direct email; exit/new joiner surveys to surface issues; external human rights channel for supply chain cases.
  - Internal investigations governed by a central Key Operating Document; proportional, independent, objective; outcomes can include policy/process changes, controls enhancements, lessons learned, disciplinary actions.
  - Anti-retaliation framework, regular training, and Anti-Retaliation Advisory Group (bi-weekly) to prevent, detect and act on retaliation.
  - Compliance with EU Whistleblowing Directive; 2024 updates clarified employees’ rights to contact authorities; localized guidance provided.
  - Training: mandatory Speak-Up/Listen Up for managers (annual refresh); Code of Conduct (every 18–24 months) and Risk Awareness (bi-annually) for all staff; 2024 completion rates: 99.98% (Code), 100% (Managers’ duties), 99.99% (Risk Awareness).
- Code of Conduct:
  - Foundation for ethical behavior; overseen by CICC; updated in 2024 to align with “This is Deutsche Bank.”
  - Covers speaking up, decision-making, conflicts of interest, financial crime, sustainability/human rights, and market integrity; annual review via cross-bank working groups; published internally and externally.
  - Supplier Code of Conduct referenced (see Supply Chain Management section).
- Culture, Integrity and Conduct program:
  - Operationalizes the Code via an annual, bank-wide book of work; focuses on ethical behavior, speak-up, and high conduct standards across businesses and functions.
  - Divisional/function culture plans include mandatory and unit-specific initiatives; quarterly progress reporting with evidence; 74 initiatives delivered in 2024.
- “This is Deutsche Bank” (TiDB) program:
  - Bank-wide change-the-bank program launched 2023; 2024 activities included communication, embedding into processes and revised Code; creation of a Culture dashboard for ongoing measurement by CICC.
  - Aspirational culture: empower employees to excel together; four guiding principles (responsibility/trust, commercial thinking/sustainability, initiative/solutions, collaboration/impact) with 16 supporting behaviors.
- Metrics and targets:
  - CICC quarterly reviews of 25 culture/conduct metrics (complaints, policy adherence, investigation outcomes, survey insights); actions taken on trends.
  - People Survey used to gauge culture (commitment, enablement, ethics, raising concerns); 2024 results indicate strong ability to express views and awareness of how to raise concerns; findings feed into the book of work and unit culture plans.
  - Annual global and divisional Culture, Integrity and Conduct reports assess progress and set next year’s agenda.
- Whistleblowing outcomes:
  - Cases referred to investigation highest in Germany, then APAC, UK & Ireland, Americas, Europe, Middle East & Africa.
  - 52% of cases closed in 2024 were partially or fully substantiated (2023: 38%).
- Anti-financial crime (AFC) overview:
  - Highlights societal harms from financial crime (fraud, bribery/corruption, terrorist financing, money laundering, sanctions evasion, internal fraud, tax evasion) and criminals’ cross-border laundering methods.
  - Governance: everyone responsible for prevention, detection, reporting; Group Anti-Money Laundering Officer heads AFC, delegated by the Management Board, reporting to the Compliance/AFC MB member; independent AFC function sets policy; businesses operationalize; regular reporting to Supervisory Board Audit Committee.
  - Strategy: uniform approach across prevention, detection, reporting; focus on remediation, simplification, consolidation; evolve AFC program in risk appetite, assessment, policy, training, assurance, and reporting; aim to accelerate risk decisions, enforce consistency, collaborate across divisions/regions, and operate within risk appetite.

structure.title: Anti-financial crime
structure.heading: Anti-financial crime
structure.start_phrase:
Financial crime is detrimental to society and can have severe negative consequences for individuals, institutions, and the 
integrity of the financial system.
structure.summary:
- Focus: Deutsche Bank’s governance, strategy, risk management, controls, partnerships, and metrics for anti-financial crime (AFC), plus governance and controls for anti-competitive behavior.

- Financial crime context and commitment:
  - Financial crime harms society; risks include money laundering, terrorist financing, sanctions evasion, bribery/corruption, internal/external fraud, and facilitation of tax evasion.
  - AFC is integral to strategy, aiming to protect clients, society, and the bank, with continuous improvement and technology/analytics enablement.

- Governance (AFC):
  - All employees are responsible for prevention, detection, and reporting.
  - Ultimate authority resides with the Group Anti-Money Laundering Officer (heads AFC, delegated by Management Board, reports to Compliance/AFC MB member); Supervisory Board receives regular updates.
  - AFC sets independent policies/standards; business divisions implement; three lines of defense model; strong speak-up and training culture.

- Strategy (AFC):
  - Uniform global strategy across prevention, detection, reporting; focuses on remediation, simplification, consolidation.
  - Evolves program elements: risk appetite, dynamic risk assessment, policy, training, assurance, and reporting; accelerates decisions, enforces consistency, strengthens risk ownership.

- Impact, risk and opportunity management (AFC):
  - Comprehensive Financial Crime Risk Management framework; annual enterprise-wide risk assessments across entities, products, services, channels, geographies; strict due diligence for lending/investment.
  - AFC involved in new products/businesses to align with risk appetite; monitors legal changes and translates into policy.
  - Resourcing: AFC headcount 2,492 at YE 2024 (2,397 in 2023) + ~900 contingent workers; 2022–2024 hiring drive strengthened execution.
  - Regulator-driven remediation continued in 2024: enhancements in governance, risk appetite/assessment, KYC, affiliate oversight, transaction monitoring/filtering, controls testing; focus on sustainable BAU.
  - Secondary sanctions risk (U.S., Russia military-industrial base): enhanced controls but residual risk cannot be eliminated; ongoing testing and adherence tracking.
  - Benefits: improved trust, market access, brand value, efficiency via consistent standards and better information sharing.

- Partnerships:
  - Active roles in Wolfsberg Group (co-chair 2024), German Anti-Financial Crime Alliance Board, Europol FIU public-private partnership (steering group), UK JMLITF, and Germany’s EuroDaT/safeAML information-sharing project.

- Policies and frameworks:
  - Framework covers ML/TF/tax evasion, sanctions/embargoes, fraud, bribery/corruption; aligned with Code of Conduct, Risk Management Policy, Risk Appetite.
  - Key global policies: AML (incl. CTF and prevention of facilitation of tax evasion), Sanctions, Anti-Bribery & Corruption (ABC), Anti-Fraud; global minimum standards with local supplements; annual reviews; mandatory training; disciplinary consequences for breaches.

- AML/CTF/Tax evasion controls:
  - Risk-based KYC/CDD (including UBO, source of funds/wealth, residency), transaction monitoring, screening, alert investigation, suspicious activity reporting, and client risk reduction/exits.
  - KYC policy details timing of reviews, PEP handling, high tax-evasion risk clients, business restrictions, and exit processes.

- Sanctions compliance:
  - Adheres to UN/EU/Germany and stricter regimes where operating (notably U.S./UK).
  - Controls: transaction filtering, client/counterparty screening, restricted instruments, rejects/freezes, activity restrictions and exits; stricter local rules override, otherwise global policy prevails.

- Fraud, bribery, and corruption:
  - ABC program aligned with UN Convention; annual inherent risk and control assessments.
  - Coverage of high-risk areas: gifts/entertainment, donations, hiring, JVs/strategic investments, vendors, books/records, political contributions.
  - Reduced reliance on high-risk business development consultants; enhanced approvals, due diligence, ABC contractual clauses, and monitoring.
  - Independent investigations; disciplinary actions up to termination; reporting to senior management and regulators as needed.
  - Fraud Risk Management framework across three lines; Anti-Fraud Policy defines fraud and escalation; first-line controls include online banking monitoring and call-backs.

- Metrics and targets (training and enforcement):
  - Mandatory annual global training for employees and contractors covering AML/CTF/CPF, sanctions, ABC, and preventing facilitation of tax evasion; non-completion escalated for disciplinary review.
  - 2024 completion rates: Anti-Fraud/Bribery/Corruption 99.88% (103,112 staff), AML/CTF/PF 99.82% (104,605), Preventing Facilitation of Tax Evasion 99.98% (51,305; two-year cycle), Sanctions 99.52% (104,157); 2023 figures excluded vendor staff.
  - 2024: no convictions or fines for anti-corruption/anti-bribery violations.

- Anti-competitive behavior:
  - Governance: Code of Conduct (MB-approved), Management Board oversight; Compliance and Legal as independent control functions; Non-Financial Risk Committee oversight; senior business management implements controls.
  - Strategy and risk management: adherence to competition laws; three lines of defense; antitrust risk integrated into annual risk/control assessments with Compliance monitoring; ongoing control enhancements.
  - Risks: potential legal/reputational impact given scale, complexity, and regulatory scrutiny.
  - Culture and response: zero tolerance, strong speak-up culture; independent investigations; disciplinary actions up to termination; reporting of breaches to senior management and authorities.

structure.title: Anti-competitive behavior
structure.heading: Anti-competitive behavior
structure.start_phrase: Deutsche Bank recognizes that managing antitrust risk effectively is integral to its governance and corporate culture.
structure.summary:
- Scope: Governance disclosures aligned with ESRS for anti-competitive behavior and tax in Deutsche Bank’s 2024 Annual Report.

- Anti-competitive behavior (Antitrust):
  - Governance and accountability: Antitrust risk embedded in the Code of Conduct; responsibility spans the Management Board and all employees. Oversight via Compliance and Legal (second line), with group-wide coordination by the Non-Financial Risk Committee and a dedicated antitrust operating forum that meets bimonthly and escalates to the Group Compliance Officer, Group General Counsel, and the Management Board.
  - Strategy and risk framework: Three Lines of Defense model; antitrust designated a key non-financial risk; annual inherent risk and controls assessments; ongoing monitoring and control enhancements; risk remains within tolerance.
  - Policy framework: Bank-wide Antitrust Risk Management Framework Policy (read with the Code of Conduct), reviewed annually and accessible to all staff; defines risk manifestations and minimum standards; covers collusive behavior, competitor information exchange, trade associations and external committees, HR-related aspects, joint ventures and cooperation; clear escalation and reporting channels.
  - Controls and culture: Preventive and detective controls (e.g., third-party interactions, contracts, monitoring); speak-up culture and whistleblowing; independent investigations; disciplinary actions up to termination; reporting of breaches to senior management and regulators; tracking of effectiveness through annual assessments and governance processes.
  - Training and enforcement: Mandatory global e-learning refreshed in 2024 with new scenarios; completion rate above 99.9%; supplementary tailored trainings; Red Flag process ties training adherence to promotions, compensation, and performance; updated Code of Conduct and training include anti-competitive behavior scenarios; ongoing updates to internal guidance and templates; reference to material proceedings in Note 27.

- Tax:
  - Governance: Independent in-house tax function as a risk and control function led by the Global Head of Tax, reporting to the CFO; Management Board and CFO approve the tax strategy and tax principles policy framework.
  - Strategy and principles: Conduct tax affairs to generate sustainable value while complying with laws and respecting the intent and spirit of tax legislation, social context, and the bank’s reputation; principles apply across all businesses, regions, and entities; align tax outcomes with the economic, regulatory, and commercial substance of activities, considering tax authorities’ perspectives; strict prohibition on aiding or abetting tax evasion (linked to Anti-Financial Crime framework).
  - Risk management and operations: Control framework to ensure material compliance, accurate filings, and timely payment; proactive, transparent, professional engagement with tax authorities; no tax advice to clients; new product approval embeds tax principles and assumes client compliance; expectation that third-party providers also comply; staffed with skilled professionals to maintain robust positions on the bank’s own tax matters.

structure.title: Tax
structure.heading: Tax
structure.start_phrase:
The bank has clear principles of conduct and behavior as they relate to the bank’s tax affairs and a framework setting out 
roles and responsibilities among the various functions for defined tax types to ensure that the bank remains compliant with 
its tax o bligations.
structure.summary:
- Tax governance and strategy:
  - Independent in-house Tax function, led by the Global Head of Tax reporting to the CFO; separate from business divisions.
  - Tax strategy and tax principles policy framework are defined with Management Board support and approved by the CFO and Management Board; published externally.
  - Core principles: generate sustainable value while complying with legal and regulatory requirements; respect the intent/spirit of tax laws and broader social/reputational considerations; consistent application across all regions and entities.
  - Zero tolerance for tax evasion; strict prohibition on aiding or abetting it (linked to Anti-Financial Crime policies).

- Tax risk management, operations, and stakeholder approach:
  - Control framework to ensure material compliance, accurate filings, timely payment, and proactive, transparent engagement with tax authorities.
  - The bank does not provide tax advice to clients; new product approval embeds tax compliance expectations for clients; similar expectations for third-party providers.
  - Ongoing monitoring of legislative changes; routine updates to policies and procedures.

- Key regulatory developments and impacts:
  - EU listing of Russia as non-cooperative jurisdiction (effective 2024) expected to have no material impact on the bank’s Russia operations.
  - OECD BEPS Pillar 2 (Global Anti-Base Erosion) 15% minimum tax: EU directive implemented and transposed into German MinStG; generally effective for tax years beginning after Dec 30, 2023; 2024 Pillar 2 reports/returns due June 2026. Deutsche Bank monitoring enactment status across countries and implications.

- Tax positioning and reporting:
  - Profits reported and taxed where generated; intercompany transactions on arm’s length basis per OECD transfer pricing.
  - No use of uncommercial artificial steps for tax benefits.
  - Country-by-country reporting derived from IFRS Group accounts but not directly reconcilable due to Bundesbank guidance (e.g., cross-border intragroup eliminations handled differently; intra-group dividends included in country results and often tax-exempt), which can affect jurisdictional effective tax rates.
  - 2024 totals: income tax expense €1.8 billion; income taxes paid €1.4 billion.
  - References provided to Notes on Income Taxes, Country-by-country reporting, and Shareholdings for further detail.

- Public policy and regulation governance:
  - Structured framework to manage regulatory change and policy engagement; supports informed strategic decisions and oversight of regulatory implementation.
  - Government & Public Affairs sits within Corporate & Strategy Affairs (CA&S); Global Head of CA&S reports to the CEO; ~19 FTE across Frankfurt, London, New York, Berlin, Brussels, Washington.
  - Close collaboration with the Regulatory & Exam Management Group (also in CA&S): principal contact with supervisors, manages exams, requests, documentation, findings, and closure.

- Public policy and regulatory strategy:
  - Systematic prioritization of regulatory risks; clear accountability for identifying changes, impact assessment, and ensuring compliance.
  - Sustainability regulations significantly shape strategy: EU Taxonomy, CSRD, SFDR, CSDDD, German Supply Chain Due Diligence Act, California GHG disclosure laws, Singapore Transition Taxonomy.
  - Support for transition to sustainable economies; advocacy for practical, comparable, and interoperable rules to improve usability of ESG disclosures.
  - Engagement with policymakers and stakeholders globally; provides thought leadership and client advisory aligned with the Global Hausbank strategy.
  - Acts as intermediary between clients and policymakers—communicating implementation challenges and clarifying regulatory intent to facilitate an effective, efficient sustainable transition.

structure.title: Public policy and regulation
structure.heading: Public policy and regulation
structure.start_phrase:
Deutsche Bank has a clearly structured framework for managing the risk of regulatory change and enhancing its profile in 
policy and regulatory debates.
structure.summary:
- Public policy and regulation framework and governance
  - Deutsche Bank’s structured framework to manage regulatory change, engage stakeholders, and oversee implementation of key regulatory initiatives.
  - Government & Public Affairs housed in Corporate & Strategy Affairs (~19 FTE across Frankfurt, London, New York, Berlin, Brussels, Washington), reporting to the Global Head of Corporate Affairs & Strategy, who reports to the CEO.
  - Close coordination with the Regulatory & Exam Management Group (principal contact for supervisors; exam management, findings, closure), also in Corporate & Strategy Affairs.

- Strategy and focus areas
  - Systematic prioritization of regulatory risks; clear accountability for identifying, assessing, and ensuring compliance.
  - Sustainability regulations shaping strategy: EU Taxonomy, CSRD, SFDR, CSDDD, German Supply Chain Act, California GHG disclosure laws, Singapore Transition Taxonomy.
  - Aim to harmonize global guidelines for comparability and transparency; act as intermediary between clients and policymakers to translate implementation challenges and regulatory intent.
  - Position papers aligned with the bank’s net‑zero strategy and Paris Agreement; emphasis on financing transition, including high‑emitting sectors with credible pathways.

- 2024 policy environment and regional priorities
  - Elections (EU Parliament, UK, US) slowed new policymaking for much of 2024, with sustainability focus picking up late in the year.
  - European Union: implementation of final Basel III, macroprudential framework review, MiFID revisions, settlement cycle work, securitization framework revisions; support for digital euro (ECB preparation and legislative framework); Instant Payments Regulation; Payment Services Directive review; call for a holistic, competitive EU payments vision; advocacy on financing Europe’s digital and sustainable transition via deeper capital markets; investor protection and Retail Investment Strategy; centrality of transition finance.
  - United Kingdom: continued financial services reforms post-government change; Listing Act changes (in force July 29, 2024), Prospectus Regime updates, Pensions Review input; secondary market focus (Wholesale Markets Review, MiFIR transparency); contribution to T+1 settlement taskforce; support for sector-specific transition plan guidance; engagement on digital gilts and broader digitalization.
  - United States: focus on prudential regulators’ Basel III “endgame” proposal raising capital for >$100bn banks; uncertainty on finalization and timing; exploration of liquidity requirement changes after March 2023 banking stress.

- Impact, risk, and opportunity management
  - Detection of regulatory developments via direct policymaker engagement, trade associations, and internal monitoring with daily updates.
  - Continuous engagement through full policy cycles; sharing insights with clients and gathering feedback on implementation hurdles to inform policymakers.
  - Advocacy for ESG‑effective, efficient rules that enable growth while respecting environmental and social needs; positioning Deutsche Bank as a sustainability leader.
  - Transition finance stance: need principle-based guidance tied to sectoral net‑zero roadmaps; make EU Taxonomy more workable; support with industrial policy.
  - CSDDD position: supportive but advocating risk-based, proportionate, low‑bureaucracy application; limit scope for financial services to loans to direct clients; highlight competitiveness concerns versus non‑covered markets.

- Advocacy governance, transparency, and memberships
  - Mission-driven Government & Public Affairs mandate to advocate for strong European banks, responsible capital markets growth, fair green transition, and payments/tech innovation.
  - Strict policies for regulator and policymaker interactions: Supervisory Authorities Engagement Policy (logging/recording), Representation of Interests Policy (German Federal Government, Parliament, EU institutions), U.S. lobbying and PAC rules.
  - Registrations: EU Transparency Register and German Federal/Bavaria/Baden‑Württemberg Lobbying Registers; disclosure of advocacy expenditures and adherence to codes of conduct.
  - No direct political donations per Group Policy; note of indirect political contributions by two non-financial trade associations in Germany (€36,254) without bank involvement.
  - Broad trade association participation (e.g., BdB, AFME, VdP, UK Finance, ISDA, SIFMA, IIF, ASIFMA); CEO Christian Sewing presides over BdB and EBF (until Feb 2025), advocating digital and sustainable transformation and Capital Markets Union.
  - Influence on regulation considered medium; impacts materialize over time; no specific advocacy KPIs—engagement aligned to mission and Global Hausbank strategy.

- Data protection (privacy) program
  - Commitment to protecting personal data under GDPR and similar laws, recognizing privacy as a fundamental social value.
  - Governance: Group Data Privacy as independent Second Line of Defense; sets principles, policies, and minimum control standards; local Data Protection Officers network; Chief Data Privacy Officer reports to the Chief Legal Officer (Management Board member).
  - Collaboration with Technology, Data and Innovation and Information Security on controls (e.g., encryption, access rights).
  - Strategy and execution: privacy embedded in culture and conduct; continuous enhancement of policies and controls, including AI initiatives.
  - 2024 actions: launch of a group-wide framework of key data protection principles; revision of the global data protection policy to strengthen roles/responsibilities; planned 2025 update to consolidate and add country specifics.
  - Ongoing regulatory monitoring, control implementation, advice on lawful processing (including third parties), employee training and awareness campaigns.
  - Industry engagement via BdB and EBF to align standards, share best practices, and reflect evolving regulatory expectations (e.g., standard privacy notices, T&Cs).

structure.title: Data protection
structure.heading: Data protection
structure.start_phrase: In most countries Deutsche Bank conducts business there is a data protection (also referenced as “data privacy”) law.
structure.summary:
- Purpose and commitment: Deutsche Bank views data protection as a core social value and legal obligation, committing to GDPR and equivalent global laws grounded in human rights frameworks.
- Governance setup: Group Data Privacy operates as an independent Second Line of Defense, with the Chief Data Privacy Officer reporting to the Chief Legal Officer (Management Board). Local Data Protection Officers support country operations. The function collaborates closely with Technology, Data and Innovation and the Chief Security Office and participates in business forums and worker council matters.
- Policy and strategy: Data protection is embedded in culture and conduct. In 2024, the bank issued a group-wide framework of key data protection principles and revised its global policy to clarify responsibilities, with a 2025 update planned to consolidate country-specific requirements. Group Data Privacy acts as the SME for legal interpretation and continuous regulatory monitoring.
- Risk and control framework: Data protection is a material topic due to reputational, legal, operational, and trust risks. Minimum control standards require notification of new personal data processing (including AI), integration into new product approval and third-party risk management, and ongoing assurance testing. Coverage of vendor risk management was expanded in 2024; no major deficiencies were identified.
- Transparency and data subject rights: The bank mandates privacy notices for clients and employees, lawful consent mechanisms, and timely handling of data subject requests. Suppliers processing personal data must meet contractual data protection obligations; Group Data Privacy supports on individual requests and complaints.
- Regulatory developments monitored in 2024: Swiss-U.S. Data Privacy Framework adequacy, amendments to Turkey’s PDPL, additional U.S. state privacy laws; ongoing monitoring of the UK DPDI Bill and EU digital and cybersecurity initiatives (e.g., ePrivacy).
- Training and awareness: Mandatory global data protection eLearning for all employees and eligible contractors was enhanced in 2024 to address new laws and AI-related risks; completion rate was 99.29% (vs. 99.96% in 2023). Ongoing awareness includes targeted trainings, newsletters, and joint initiatives with Information Security; non-compliance may lead to disciplinary action.
- Incident management and reporting: Group Data Privacy monitors potential personal data breaches and coordinates with the global security incident process, advising on regulatory notifications and informing affected individuals when required. No personal data breaches of material impact to individuals were observed in 2024.
- Reporting frameworks: The section aligns with ESRS (e.g., GOV-2, SBM-3, IRO-1/2, S1, S4) and GRI (404-2/FS4, 418-1) disclosures.
- Information security reference: Detailed information security governance, strategy, and risk management are provided in the Annual Report’s Risk Report under Risk and Capital Management.

2024 included in the Combined Management Report section of Deutsche Bank’s Annual Report.
structure.summary:
- EY issued a limited assurance report on Deutsche Bank’s 2024 group sustainability statement, which is included in the Combined Management Report and combined with the parent company’s sustainability statement.
- Scope and criteria: Assurance against CSRD (Directive (EU) 2022/2464), EU Taxonomy Article 8 (Regulation (EU) 2020/852), and German Commercial Code sections 289b–289e and 315b–315c, with reference to the company’s elaborative criteria.
- Conclusion: Nothing came to the auditor’s attention indicating the statement is not prepared, in all material respects, in accordance with CSRD, EU Taxonomy Article 8, ESRS, and that the materiality assessment aligns with the description in the Double materiality statement section.
- Assurance basis: Engagement performed under ISAE 3000 (Revised); independence affirmed; quality management under IDW QMS 1 and ISQM 1; limited assurance provides a lower level of assurance than reasonable assurance.
- Management and oversight responsibilities: Executive directors are responsible for preparation, internal controls, materiality assessment, methods, estimates, and forward-looking information; the Supervisory Board oversees the preparation process.
- Inherent limitations: Ongoing interpretation uncertainties in CSRD and related requirements may affect legal conformity; such limitations also affect the assurance work.
- Auditor responsibilities and procedures: Understanding of the preparation and materiality processes; risk-based focus on potential misstatements (including higher risk in value chain data); evaluation of forward-looking assumptions; assessment of methods, estimates, presentation; analytical procedures and inquiries; assessment of EU Taxonomy eligibility/alignment processes. Where value chain data are estimated per ESRS after reasonable efforts, auditors evaluate the estimation approach and reasonableness rather than determining the data themselves.
- Use and liability: Report intended for the company’s purposes only; not for third-party decision-making; liability to third parties disclaimed per General Engagement Terms (1 January 2024); no obligation to update the report after issuance unless required by law.
- Formalities: Report dated March 10, 2025, issued by EY GmbH & Co. KG, signed by two German Public Auditors.
- ESRS content index: Introduction to the list of ESRS disclosure requirements complied with, stating the Sustainability Statement’s comprehensive coverage based on a 2024 double materiality assessment and compliance with all listed ESRS requirements; index maps ESRS 1 and ESRS 2 (including GOV-1, GOV-2, BP-1, BP-2, and general disclosures) to chapters such as Governance, Supply chain management (including Asset Management), Own workforce, Client centricity, Anti-financial crime, and Anti-competitive behavior, with page references.

structure.summary:

- ESRS content index: A detailed mapping of each ESRS standard and disclosure requirement to the relevant Sustainability Statement chapter and page. It covers ESRS 1 (general requirements) and ESRS 2 (general disclosures) across:
  - Governance (roles of administrative/management/supervisory bodies, information flows, incentive schemes, due diligence, internal controls over sustainability reporting).
  - Identification and assessment of material impacts, risks and opportunities.
  - Strategy, business model, value chain, stakeholder interests and engagement.
  - Policies, actions/resources, metrics, and targets for all material topics.

  - Climate change (ESRS E1) including the transition plan, policies, actions, targets, and financed emissions (Scope 3 Category 15), plus Asset Management portfolio metrics/targets.
  - Governance (ESRS G1) including corporate culture, supplier management, anti-corruption/bribery (incidents and prevention/detection), political influence/lobbying, and payment practices.
  - Own workforce (ESRS S1) including policies, engagement and remediation channels, workforce management, working conditions (talent development, performance/reward, work-life balance), diversity/equity/inclusion (gender, age, ethnicity, disability), pay metrics, incidents/complaints, and targets.
  - Consumers and end-users (ESRS S4) including product responsibility, selling/marketing practices, client satisfaction, complaint management, and remediation channels.
  - Additional material topics: sustainable finance across divisions, ESG due diligence (incl. Equator Principles), supply chain management, client centricity, culture/integrity/conduct, anti-financial crime, anti-competitive behavior, tax, public policy and regulation, data protection, and information security.

- Regulatory linkages: A separate table identifies ESRS datapoints that derive from other EU legislation (SFDR, CRR/Pillar 3 Article 449a, Benchmark Regulation, EU Climate Law), with references and reporting locations. Items include board diversity/independence, due diligence statements, involvement in fossil fuels/chemicals/controversial weapons/tobacco, the 2050 climate-neutral transition plan, Paris-aligned Benchmark exclusions, GHG reduction targets, and energy consumption/intensity (not material).

structure.start_phrase:
The table below illustrates the datapoints in ESRS 2 and topical ESRS that derive from other EU legislation as required in 
ESRS 2 Appendix B.
structure.summary:
- Purpose: A comprehensive cross‑reference table required by ESRS 2 Appendix B that maps ESRS 2 and topical ESRS disclosure datapoints to corresponding requirements in other EU legislation and shows where Deutsche Bank reports them in its Sustainability Statement.
- Regulations mapped: SFDR (Annex I indicators), CRR Article 449a Pillar 3 climate/social risk templates (Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2453), the Benchmark Regulation delegated acts (EU) 2020/1816 and 2020/1818, and the EU Climate Law (Regulation (EU) 2021/1119).
- What the table provides for each datapoint: the ESRS reference, associated SFDR indicator numbers/tables, Pillar 3 templates/paragraphs, Benchmark/Climate Law clauses, the Sustainability Statement chapter title, and an explicit note on materiality/relevance (e.g., material, not material, not applicable, not relevant for 2024).
- Governance (ESRS 2 GOV): Board gender diversity and independence (linked to SFDR and Benchmark Reg.), and a due diligence statement (mapped to SFDR PAI), reported under Corporate Governance and ESG due diligence.
- Strategy/business model (ESRS 2 SBM-1): Involvement in fossil fuels, chemical production, controversial weapons, and tobacco tied to SFDR and Benchmark Reg.; most marked “Not applicable” for chapter placement.
- Climate (ESRS E1):  
  - Transition plan to 2050 and GHG targets mapped to EU Climate Law, SFDR, Benchmark Reg., and Pillar 3; reported under Sustainability Strategy/Climate change – Transition plan.  
  - GHG emissions (Scope 1–3): SFDR and Pillar 3 linkages; only Scope 3 Category 15 (financed emissions) is material (reported under Client portfolios – Metrics and targets), others not material.  
  - Energy consumption/mix/intensity mostly “Not material.”  
  - Physical risk exposure, asset location, and real estate energy efficiency templates flagged “Not relevant for 2024.”  
  - Climate‑related opportunities linked to Benchmark Reg., reported under Sustainable Finance.
- Pollution (ESRS E2), Water & Marine (ESRS E3), Biodiversity (ESRS E4), and Resource use/Circular economy (ESRS E5): Multiple SFDR indicators referenced (e.g., E‑PRTR emissions, water consumption/recycling, deforestation and oceans policies, non‑recycled and hazardous waste), largely assessed “Not material.”
- Own workforce (ESRS S1): Policies and due diligence on human rights/ILO conventions, anti‑trafficking, accident prevention, grievance mechanisms, diversity and pay equity, and incidents of discrimination; mapped to SFDR and Benchmark Reg.; reporting spread across workforce‑related chapters (DEI, work‑life balance, remediation channels). Several quantitative safety metrics noted “Not material.”
- Workers in the value chain (ESRS S2) and Affected communities (ESRS S3): Human rights policy commitments, due diligence, risks of child/forced labor, non‑respect of UNGPs/OECD, and incident reporting mapped to SFDR/Benchmark Reg.; most items “Not material.”
- Consumers and end‑users (ESRS S4): Policies, non‑respect of UNGPs/OECD, and incidents tied to SFDR/Benchmark Reg.; disclosures located in Client centricity (product responsibility, client satisfaction, complaint management).
- Business conduct (ESRS G1): Anti‑corruption (UN Convention), whistleblower protection, fines, and standards mapped to SFDR/Benchmark Reg.; reported under Anti‑financial crime and Culture, integrity and conduct.
- Overall: The table demonstrates regulatory alignment, traceability across EU frameworks, and Deutsche Bank’s materiality conclusions and reporting locations for each ESRS‑linked datapoint for the 2024 reporting year.
